options: Move Where before ToList: `db.Users.Where(u => u.Age > 30).ToList()` to filter in the database
Use AsParallel() to parallelize the client-side filtering
Add an index on the Age column
Use SqlParameter instead of a LINQ where clause
explanation: LINQ providers defer to the database until you call ToList(); filtering before ToList ensures the WHERE happens in SQL, not in memory.

question: You profile a web request and find most time is in String concatenation: `string query = "SELECT * FROM " + table + " WHERE id=" + id;` What is the fix and why?
options: Use string interpolation or StringBuilder for multiple concatenations to avoid creating intermediate strings
Use regular expressions to speed up the string building
Compile the query once and reuse it
Concatenation is already optimized by the compiler so this is not the bottleneck
explanation: String concatenation with + creates temporary strings for each operation; interpolation and StringBuilder reduce allocations significantly.

question: A method allocates a 1MB array every call in a tight loop. Why is object pooling better than relying on GC?
options: Pooling reuses memory across iterations, reducing GC pressure and pauses; allocating fresh each time triggers frequent collections
Object pooling prevents all garbage collection completely
GC is always slower than pooling
Arrays are exempt from garbage collection
explanation: Frequent allocations in tight loops trigger GC pauses; pooling reuses buffers and reduces heap pressure dramatically.

question: You notice a method checking `if(someList.Count > 0)` before operations. On a LinkedList, why is this slower than `if(!someList.Any())`?
options: LinkedList.Count is O(n) because it walks the entire list; Any() short-circuits after one element
LinkedList.Count has a slower CPU instruction than Any()
Any() uses SIMD instructions while Count does not
Count always allocates a temporary collection
explanation: LinkedList.Count iterates all nodes; Any() checks existence by accessing the head, returning immediately — O(1) vs O(n).

question: Why should you use `readonly` on reference-type fields that never change?
options: Compiler can elide null checks and avoid repeated memory lookups in loops, plus prevents accidental reassignment
Readonly prevents garbage collection
Readonly makes the field thread-safe
Readonly reduces the field size in memory
explanation: Readonly fields signal immutability to the compiler and JIT, enabling escape analysis and eliding repeated dereferences in hot code.

question: An N-query EF Core loop: `foreach(var id in ids) { var item = db.Items.First(x => x.Id == id); }` loads one-by-one. What is the optimized query?
options: Use `db.Items.Where(x => ids.Contains(x.Id)).ToDictionary(x => x.Id)` to load all in one query and look up by key
Use `db.Items.AsNoTracking().ToList()` to disable change tracking
Execute queries in parallel with Parallel.ForEach
Use a stored procedure instead of LINQ
explanation: Batch loading with Contains avoids N round-trips to the database; dictionary lookup is O(1) per ID.

question: A struct with 200 bytes is used as a method parameter and returned by value. What is the downside and the fix?
options: Large structs are copied on stack push/return causing perf loss; pass by reference with `ref` or convert to a class
Structs are always faster than classes
Method parameters are never copied in C#
Returning by value prevents stack unwinding
explanation: Value types are copied entirely on assignment and parameter passing; large structs cause cache misses and register pressure unless passed by ref.

question: A loop repeatedly calls `string.Empty.Length`. Why can the JIT optimize this to a constant?
options: String.Empty is interned and immutable; the JIT replaces the property access with the literal 0 at compile time
String properties are cached by the runtime
The optimizer recognizes the method name Empty and substitutes
Access to interned strings bypasses the Length property
explanation: String.Empty is a static readonly reference to the interned empty string; the JIT inlines and recognizes it as a known constant.

question: EF Core: `.Include(x => x.Orders).ThenInclude(x => x.Items)` loads related data. When is this approach slower than two separate queries?
options: When the join result is so wide and duplicated that it exceeds network/memory gains; separate queries with manual joining may be faster
Include is always slower than multiple queries
Network latency makes separate queries impossible
ThenInclude does not actually load data from the database
explanation: Include multiplies result rows by related data; wide joins can send redundant data over the network, making separate queries with indexing faster.

question: A CPU-bound operation is split into many small tasks with Task.Run. When does the overhead outweigh the parallelism gain?
options: When task creation, scheduling, and context-switching cost more than the actual work; use Parallel.For with tuned grain size instead
When there are more tasks than CPU cores
When any task throws an exception
When running on a multi-core processor
explanation: Task scheduling has fixed overhead; too many small tasks incur context-switch and allocation costs exceeding the parallelism benefit; Parallel.For partitions dynamically.

question:
A view iterates over related objects without select_related or prefetch_related. How many queries are executed?

```python
def show_posts(request):
    posts = Post.objects.all()  # 1 query
    for post in posts:
        print(post.author.name)  # N queries for N posts (N+1 problem)
```
options: 1 query for all posts; author names are fetched in the same query
N+1 queries: 1 for posts, 1 per post for the author
2 queries: 1 for posts, 1 for all authors (via implicit JOIN)
N queries: one per post (Django batches queries internally)
explanation: Without select_related, each post.author access triggers a separate query; this is the classic N+1 problem; use select_related('author') to fetch in one query.

question:
A queryset uses prefetch_related for a ManyToMany field. How many queries are executed?

```python
posts = Post.objects.prefetch_related('tags')
for post in posts:
    for tag in post.tags.all():
        print(tag.name)
```
options: 1 query for posts, N queries for tags per post (no optimization)
2 queries: 1 for posts, 1 for all tags
N+1 queries: the prefetch is ignored because tags.all() is called
2 queries: prefetch_related batches the tags fetching
explanation: prefetch_related caches the related objects; post.tags.all() uses the cache instead of hitting the database again, so 2 queries total.

question:
A queryset uses select_related but then filters on the related object. Does this cause extra queries?

```python
posts = Post.objects.select_related('author').filter(author__is_active=True)
```
options: No extra queries; the filter is applied to the joined query
Yes, a separate query is executed for the filter
select_related fetches authors first, then filters in Python
The filter overrides select_related; the join is removed
explanation: select_related uses SQL JOIN to fetch related objects and apply filters in a single query; no extra queries are executed.

question:
A queryset is evaluated multiple times. Are results cached?

```python
users = User.objects.filter(is_active=True)
print(len(users))  # First evaluation
print(list(users))  # Second evaluation
```
options: Results are cached; the second evaluation uses the cached data
The database is queried twice; no caching occurs
Caching depends on the QuerySet backend (database vs cache)
Results are cached only within a single request
explanation: Django caches QuerySet results after the first evaluation; subsequent iterations use the cache, not new queries.

options: Connections are closed after 600 seconds of inactivity
Connections are closed after 600 seconds regardless of activity (max age)
A connection is closed after 600 requests
CONN_MAX_AGE only applies to persistent connections in production
explanation: CONN_MAX_AGE sets the maximum age in seconds; Django closes and reopens connections that exceed this age, even if active.

question:
A queryset uses values() to select specific columns. Does this improve performance?

```python
users = User.objects.values('name', 'email').all()
```
options: Yes, fewer columns are fetched from the database
No, Django always fetches all columns regardless of values()
Yes, but only if the model has a large number of fields
Performance depends on the database backend used
explanation: values() selects specific columns in SQL; the database returns only those columns, reducing data transfer and memory usage.

options: Minimal; signals are asynchronous and do not block saves
Significant; every save triggers an extra database query
Depends on the number of Profile objects
The query is cached; subsequent saves do not hit the database
explanation: Signal handlers are synchronous; every save triggers the handler immediately, causing an extra query; consider deferring with async tasks for high-traffic models.

question:
A view uses exists() to check if a record exists instead of count(). Why is this faster?

```python
# Slower
if Post.objects.filter(user=user).count() > 0:
    pass

# Faster
if Post.objects.filter(user=user).exists():
    pass
```
options: exists() returns after finding the first record; count() scans all
Both execute the same query; the performance difference is negligible
exists() uses an index; count() uses a full table scan
count() is always slower because it returns an integer
explanation: exists() returns True as soon as one record is found (LIMIT 1); count() scans all matching records and returns the total, making it slower.

question:
A queryset is sliced before evaluation. Does the slice reduce database queries?

```python
users = User.objects.filter(is_active=True)[0:10]
for user in users:
    print(user.name)
```
options: The slice is applied in SQL; only 10 rows are fetched from the database
All rows are fetched first, then sliced in Python
The slice is applied after filtering; both reduce query time
Slicing does not affect query performance; all rows are always fetched
explanation: Slicing on a QuerySet adds LIMIT/OFFSET to the SQL query; only the sliced rows are fetched from the database.

question:
A queryset uses only() to select specific fields. What happens with related lookups?

```python
post = Post.objects.only('title', 'content').select_related('author').get(pk=1)
print(post.author.name)  # Does this trigger a new query?
```
options: No extra query; select_related fetches the author
Yes, accessing author.name triggers a query because author is not in only()
The only() restriction applies to both Post and Author
only() is ignored when combined with select_related
explanation: select_related fetches the author despite only() limiting Post fields; only() does not affect select_related results.

question: A resolver fetches data using SELECT * but only 3 of 20 columns are needed. What's the performance impact?
options: No impact; unused columns are not sent to the client
Unnecessary data is loaded from disk/memory and transferred across the database connection, wasting resources
The query executes faster because SELECT * is optimized
Only the needed columns are loaded by default
explanation: Resolvers should use the info argument to fetch only requested fields; SELECT * wastes database and network resources.

question: A resolver caches results for 1 hour. A client queries the same field twice within seconds. What's the cache benefit?
options: No benefit; caches only help across multiple clients
Second request is served from cache, avoiding expensive computation or database access
Cache invalidation prevents the second request from using the cache
Caching increases latency
explanation: Request-scoped and field-level caches reduce redundant work within a request or across users.

question: A query fetches 100 users, each with 50 fields, but the client only renders 5 fields. What's the waste?
options: Network bandwidth is wasted on 45 unused fields per user
No waste; unused fields are dropped before transmission
Memory is wasted on the client
The query is automatically optimized
explanation: Over-fetching—requesting more fields than needed—wastes bandwidth; queries should request only necessary data.

question: Query response time increases linearly with the number of requested fields. What optimization is most effective?
options: Increase server RAM
Request fewer fields per query and use pagination for large collections
Use HTTP/2 multiplexing
Compress the response
explanation: Limiting fields and paginating collections directly reduces resolver calls and data transfer.

question: A resolver is called 1000 times per query with the same arguments. Without batching, how many database calls occur?
options: 1 database call
1000 database calls (N+1 problem)
10 database calls (partial batching)
The database optimizes this automatically
explanation: Without DataLoader or batching, each resolver call triggers a separate database query—the N+1 problem.

question: A schema exposes computed fields like averageRating that require complex calculations. When should this be cached?
options: Computed fields should never be cached
Cache computation results with a TTL; invalidate on source data changes
Clients should compute it locally
The database should always compute it on query
explanation: Expensive computations should be cached with appropriate invalidation; clients shouldn't recompute on every request.

question: A field resolver makes an HTTP request to an external API. Multiple queries request this field. How should this be optimized?
options: Make no optimizations; each query should independently fetch
Use a request-scoped cache or DataLoader to batch API calls within a request window
Cache responses indefinitely
Remove the field entirely
explanation: Request-scoped caches de-duplicate identical external API calls within a single request, reducing latency and API load.

question: A schema has query complexity defined per field. How should this be used?
options: Complexity is informational only
Reject queries exceeding a complexity budget to prevent resource exhaustion
Complexity is automatically enforced by GraphQL
It only applies to mutations
explanation: Query complexity analysis rejects expensive queries before execution; complexity budgets prevent denial-of-service attacks.

question: A resolver's performance degrades as the database grows. What's the root cause and solution?
options: No optimization is possible
Missing database indices; query plan changes with data volume—add indices on frequently queried fields
GraphQL is inherently slow
The resolver logic is inefficient
explanation: Database query plans change as tables grow; indices on queried columns maintain performance at scale.

question: Resolver execution time is dominated by waiting for database queries. What optimization would help most?
options: Use Redis to cache all query results
Implement DataLoader and connection pooling to batch and parallelize database calls
Increase the query timeout
Switch to a faster language
explanation: DataLoader batches queries and connection pooling parallelizes them; both reduce latency from blocking database calls.

question: You have 1000 items in a v-for loop and only 20 are visible in the viewport. Which approach best optimizes rendering performance?
options: Use v-show instead of v-if to keep all items in the DOM but hidden
Implement virtual scrolling to render only visible items and dynamic range as the user scrolls
Render all 1000 items at once; Vue's diffing algorithm handles performance
Split the list into smaller arrays and lazy-load chunks with pagination
explanation: Virtual scrolling renders only visible items in a windowed range, drastically reducing DOM nodes and improving performance for large lists.

question: A component has many computed properties. Each depends on a single reactive value. When that value updates, how many computed properties recalculate?
options: All of them recalculate to ensure consistency
Only those whose dependency actually changed; Vue tracks dependency graphs and skips unaffected computeds
Vue recalculates them lazily when accessed; those not accessed skip calculation
Only the first one; others must be manually invalidated
explanation: Vue's dependency tracking is granular; each computed property recalculates only if its dependencies changed, enabling fine-grained optimization.

question: Your component renders a large render function. You want to memoize it to avoid re-rendering on prop changes. Which approach is correct?
options: Wrap the render function in `computed(() => renderFunction())`
Use `defineComponent({ inheritAttrs: false })` to disable attribute updates
Wrap it in `memo()` or use `defineComponent({ props: [...], emits: [...], memo: true })`
Render functions are not memoizable in Vue 3
explanation: Use the `memo()` helper or `defineComponent({ ... })` with skipped props to skip re-renders when props have not changed.

question: You define a reactive variable that is read by 50 components. Updating it triggers 50 component re-renders. How do you batch them into one update cycle?
options: Vue automatically batches synchronous updates; only one re-render occurs if all 50 reads happen synchronously
Use `batch()` API to group multiple updates into a single render cycle
Updates are not batched; each component re-renders independently
Move the reactive state into Vuex; stores provide automatic batching
explanation: Vue batches synchronous updates into a single re-render cycle; only one flush to the DOM occurs even if 50 components update.

question: You import a heavy component: `const Component = () => import('./Heavy.vue')`. On each render, does Vue re-import the module?
options: Yes, the import runs on each render, loading the component repeatedly
No, the module is cached by the bundler after the first import; subsequent renders reuse it
Only if the component is removed from the DOM; cached while rendered
Depends on the bundler; Webpack caches, but Vite does not
explanation: Module imports are cached by the bundler after the first load; subsequent renders use the cached module from memory.

question: A component defines a reactive variable inside render: `const state = reactive({ count: 0 })`. On each render, is a new reactive object created?
options: Yes, a new reactive object is created on every render, causing performance issues
No, Vue detects repeated reactive definitions and reuses the object across renders
Only the first render creates it; subsequent renders skip the reactive() call
You should move reactive outside render to prevent re-creation; defining it inside causes memory leaks
explanation: Creating reactive objects inside render is inefficient; move state definitions to setup() or component scope to avoid re-creation.

question: You wrap a slow component in `<Suspense>` with a loading #fallback. The fallback renders, then the component loads. Does the fallback stay visible while the component hydrates?
options: Yes, the fallback remains visible during hydration
No, Suspense automatically hides the fallback once the component async setup resolves, before hydration completes
The fallback is replaced immediately when async data arrives, even if rendering is still happening
Suspense keeps the fallback visible until the component is fully interactive
explanation: Suspense shows the fallback until the async setup completes; once resolved, it renders the component, even if hydration is ongoing.

question: Your app uses multiple large store modules. Only 3 are used on the current page. How do you avoid loading all modules?
options: Vuex loads all modules at startup; you cannot split them dynamically
Use lazy module registration: `store.registerModule()` on demand to load modules when needed
Move unused modules to a separate file and import only on page navigation
Use dynamic imports and provide/inject instead of a global store
explanation: Vuex supports `registerModule()` to load modules dynamically at runtime, enabling lazy loading for large stores.

question: A component reads `state.users[0]` inside a template. A watcher on `state.users` is marked deep: true. When `state.users[0].name` changes, does it fire?
options: No, watchers only track reactive property assignments, not nested mutations
Yes, deep: true traverses all nested properties; changes at any depth trigger the watcher
Yes, but with a performance penalty; deep watching slows down for large objects
Only if the mutation happens synchronously; async mutations are not detected
explanation: deep: true watches all nested properties, but it traverses the entire tree on each run—avoid for large objects; watch specific properties instead.

question: You set `shallowRef()` on a large object instead of `ref()`. Does this improve rendering performance?
options: Yes, shallowRef skips tracking nested properties, reducing reactivity overhead
No, shallowRef still triggers re-renders; the performance gain is negligible for most apps
Yes, shallowRef avoids creating nested reactive proxies, significantly reducing memory and CPU for deeply nested objects
shallowRef is deprecated in Vue 3; use reactive() instead
explanation: shallowRef only tracks the top-level ref change, not nested mutations; for large immutable objects, this avoids proxy overhead.

options: 1000, because every watcher runs every digest regardless of changes
Only changed fields' watchers run, so typically under 1000
Angular batches watchers for optimization so less than 50 run
AngularJS skips watchers that haven't changed since the last digest
explanation: Angular's digest cycle runs ALL registered watchers on every digest cycle; 1000 individual watchers means 1000 function invocations per digest, causing severe performance degradation.

question:
A template has ng-repeat with ng-if inside iterating over a large list. Does the hidden DOM exist but is invisible or is it not in the DOM? ```html
{{ item.name }}
```
options: ng-if removes the element from the DOM completely when false
ng-if hides the element with display:none but keeps it in the DOM
The hidden elements are still watched and slow down digests
ng-if creates a new scope but doesn't remove the DOM
explanation: ng-if removes elements from the DOM and unbinds watchers when the condition is false; this is more efficient than ng-show which just hides with CSS.

question:
A large list uses ng-repeat with track by $index. Why is this potentially problematic for performance? ```html
{{ item.name }}
```
options: If items are reordered or removed, DOM elements are recreated unnecessarily
track by $index is always optimal because it's the fastest lookup
The browser can't cache DOM elements when using $index
Angular disables optimizations when track by is used
explanation: track by $index ties DOM elements to array positions; if items are reordered or removed, DOM nodes are destroyed and recreated even if the items still exist; track by item.id is usually better for stable identity.

question:
A controller binds a filter to a large array in the template: {{ items | filter:search }}. Every keystroke in the search input runs the filter. How can this be optimized?
```html
<input ng-model="search">
<div ng-repeat="item in items | filter:search">
```
options: Use a debounced search that filters only after user stops typing
Move filtering to the controller and bind a pre-filtered array
Use track by to optimize the ng-repeat
Filter in the controller and rebind on input change via ng-change
explanation: Filters run on every digest; filtering large arrays in templates is inefficient; moving the filter logic to the controller and updating the filtered array on input change is faster.

options: Wrap in $q.when() and return a promise that resolves lazily
Move calculation to a lazy getter that computes on first access
Calculate in a $timeout to defer execution to the next tick
Use route resolve to defer the service instantiation
explanation: Lazy getters allow deferred computation; the service is instantiated quickly, and expensive calculations happen only when the property is accessed, not at startup.

options: Deep watches on complex objects are inefficient; refactor to watch specific properties
The updateUI function should be memoized to avoid redundant work
Angular is re-evaluating the expression on every digest unnecessarily
The listener runs too frequently because deep watch checks all properties
explanation: Deep watches are expensive because they recursively compare all properties; watching specific sub-properties or using shallow watches is more efficient.

options: Use ng-repeat's track by to preserve compiled elements across iterations
Set compile to null and move logic to link to reduce overhead
Implement a compile-time cache of processed DOM trees
Clone compiled elements instead of recompiling from scratch
explanation: ng-repeat with proper track by reuses compiled DOM elements; changing track by from $index to a stable identifier preserves elements and skips recompilation.

options: Event listeners aren't deregistered in $destroy, holding references to scope
The directive doesn't unbind watchers on destruction
ng-repeat caches old items even after they're removed
Closures in link functions capture the scope indefinitely
explanation: Event listeners created in link functions hold references to the scope; if not removed in a $destroy listener, they prevent garbage collection of the scope and its data.

options: The $destroy listener isn't properly deregistering event listeners or timers
AngularJS keeps old scopes in memory even after $destroy
ng-repeat inside the modal caches items and doesn't remove them
The modal controller doesn't null out large data objects
explanation: If event listeners, timers, or other resources aren't cleaned up in $destroy, they persist and prevent garbage collection; ensure all external references are released.

question: A large repeated list re-renders slowly on every keystroke elsewhere. Which change most reduces digest cost?
options: Use one-time bindings (::) for values that never change
Add more watchers to track changes
Wrap the list in a second ng-app
Disable ng-repeat and use innerHTML
explanation: One-time bindings remove watchers after the first stabilization, shrinking the digest loop for static data.

question: Why does normalizing state (storing items in a flat object keyed by ID instead of an array) improve performance?
options: Normalized state enables O(1) lookups by ID and reduces duplication; updates affect only the target item, not the entire array, minimizing re-renders
Normalized state slows down lookups
Arrays are always faster than objects
Normalization has no performance impact
explanation: Normalized structures decouple items; updating one doesn't change the collection reference, enabling fine-grained selector updates.

question: A selector uses reselect's createSelector with many dependencies. When performance degrades, what could be the cause?
options: Complex dependencies with many intermediate selectors create overhead; memoization overhead can exceed computation savings if recomputation is cheap; simplify dependencies
reselect always improves performance
Too many dependencies breaks memoization
reselect has a limit on dependency count
explanation: reselect memoization has overhead; if intermediate selectors change frequently, memoization thrashing wastes time—measure and optimize.

question: A list renders 1000 items, each dispatching an action on click. How can Redux help optimize this scenario?
options: Use selectors to prevent list re-renders when unrelated state changes; memoize item callbacks with useCallback; consider event delegation to reduce listener count
Redux cannot optimize list rendering
Render all items on every change
Disable Redux for large lists
explanation: Selectors + memoized callbacks + event delegation combine to minimize renders and listeners—key patterns for large lists.

question: When should you split Redux state into multiple slices managed by separate reducers, and how does this help performance?
options: Split by domain (users, posts, comments); separate slices allow independent updates and enables fine-grained selectors to skip re-renders when unrelated slices change
Always use a single monolithic reducer
Split state by component
Slices reduce performance
explanation: Slices decouple state updates; selectors can subscribe to specific slices, preventing components from re-rendering on unrelated changes.

question: A reducer copies an entire array on every update: `return {state, items: [...state.items, newItem]}`. When does this become a performance problem?
options: When items is large (1000+ elements), array spread is O(n) and happens on every action; normalized updates (adding to an object) are O(1)
Array spread is always fast
Redux forbids array spread
Performance only depends on item count, not update frequency
explanation: Array spread scales linearly; for large, frequently-updated arrays, normalization or tree structures (Immer) reduce overhead.

question: Why would using React.memo on components connected to Redux improve performance?
options: React.memo prevents re-renders if props haven't changed; Redux-connected components re-render when the store updates, so memo skips renders when selectors return the same values
React.memo makes Redux faster
Redux components cannot use memo
memo prevents Redux subscriptions
explanation: memo + memoized selectors combine to skip re-renders; memo is the component-level gate that useSelector's change detection operates through.

question: When should you prefer lazy-loading selectors (computed per component) over global memoized selectors?
options: When selectors are rarely used or computation depends on component-specific parameters; global selectors are best for shared, frequently-accessed derived data
Lazy-loading is always faster
Global selectors should never be used
Lazy-loading prevents memoization
explanation: Global selectors cache effectively for shared data; component-specific selectors are lighter for rare or parameterized computations.

question: A reducer computes a filtered list on every action, even if the source data hasn't changed. How does this waste performance, and what is the fix?
options: Re-computing a filter creates a new array every action; move filtering to a memoized selector that only recomputes when source data changes
Filtering in reducers is always correct
Selectors cannot perform filtering
Memoized selectors slow down filtering
explanation: Reducers should be simple; derived data like filtering belongs in memoized selectors to avoid wasteful re-computation.

question: When should you consider using Redux Thunk caching middleware or request deduplication?
options: When the same async action is dispatched repeatedly from multiple components in quick succession; caching prevents duplicate API calls and network overhead
Caching is always necessary
Redux handles deduplication automatically
Deduplication reduces data freshness
explanation: Deduplication middleware (or thunk conditions) prevents redundant requests, saving bandwidth and server load when multiple components fetch the same data.

question: How can subscription batching improve performance in Redux applications?
options: Batching groups multiple state updates into a single subscriber notification, reducing re-render cycles; synchronous dispatches batch automatically; async updates need batching APIs
Batching slows down Redux
Redux forbids batching
Batching is only for large applications
explanation: Batching is key to Redux performance; multiple synchronous dispatches notify subscribers once, preventing wasteful intermediate re-renders.

question: Your production CSS is 2 MB instead of 50 KB. The content array in tailwind.config.js is empty. Why is this a problem?
options: Without content paths, Tailwind includes all utilities; purging can't remove unused CSS
Empty content means Tailwind doesn't scan any files and generates no CSS
2 MB is the expected size for Tailwind CSS
Tailwind doesn't support content scanning
explanation: content paths tell Tailwind's PurgeCSS which files to scan; empty content means 'scan nothing', so all utilities are included by default.

question: Your build includes hundreds of utilities you don't use. The content array is `['./src/**/*.{js,jsx}']`. Why might utilities still be included?
options: CSS files and HTML templates aren't scanned; add ['./src/**/*.css', './public/**/*.html'] to content
Tailwind can't scan JSX files
Unused utilities are always included for safety
You must manually list utilities in config
explanation: content paths must match file types you're scanning; if utilities are in CSS classes or Tailwind is used in .html files, include those extensions.

question: You have dynamic class names: `const size = 'md'; return <div className={`p-${size}`}>`. Does Tailwind's purge include p-md?
options: No, dynamic class names via template strings are not detected by static scanning; use safelist or hardcode class names
Yes, Tailwind automatically detects dynamic classes
Only if you set dynamicAttributes: true in config
Purging doesn't affect dynamic classes
explanation: Tailwind's scanner uses regex; template strings like `p-${size}` aren't recognized as complete class names; use safelist to include them.

question: Your app bundles Tailwind CSS. Should you minify the CSS further with a tool like cssnano?
options: Tailwind's build already minifies; additional minification has minimal gains and can cause issues
Yes, always minify CSS with cssnano for best results
Only if file size exceeds 100 KB
Minification is handled by the browser
explanation: Tailwind's build outputs minified CSS; cssnano can reduce by ~2-5% more but introduces risk; rely on Tailwind's minification.

question: You load Tailwind via a CDN: `<link href="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com" rel="stylesheet">`. Why is this not recommended for production?
options: CDN-delivered Tailwind includes all utilities (full unoptimized build), creating large downloads; production must use npm + build
CDN is faster than npm
Tailwind CDN doesn't work
CDN Tailwind is only for development
explanation: Tailwind CDN delivers the full unoptimized build (~3 MB). For production, use npm + PurgeCSS to generate only used utilities.

question: You use `@apply px-4 py-2 rounded` to create many component classes. Does this increase the final CSS size compared to composing utilities in HTML?
options: Potentially yes; @apply duplicates CSS code, while HTML composition reuses utilities; @apply should be reserved for true design system components
No, @apply is more efficient than composing utilities
CSS file size is unaffected by @apply usage
Tailwind recommends @apply for all repeated patterns
explanation: @apply expands to full CSS rules; if you @apply the same utilities in 10 components, the rule repeats 10 times instead of reusing one utility class.

question: Your Tailwind build includes `shadow-xs` through `shadow-2xl` but your design only uses `shadow-md`. Should you remove unused shadows from the theme?
options: Yes, extend the theme and remove unused sizes to reduce CSS; if shadow-md is all you need, set theme.shadow: { md: '...' }
No, all shadows should be included
Unused shadows are automatically purged
Removing shadows breaks Tailwind
explanation: Manually removing unused theme values reduces output CSS; if only shadow-md is used, override theme.shadow to include only md.

question: A component library exports 500 components using Tailwind. For apps importing this library, should the library pre-purge its CSS?
options: No, component libraries should not purge; apps using the library should purge their own build including library imports
Yes, library should purge to reduce its size
Libraries can't use Tailwind
Purging is only for apps, not libraries
explanation: Libraries should ship untouched Tailwind (all utilities); consuming apps control content scanning and purging for their specific usage.

question: You enable Tailwind's `corePlugins: false` and manually enable only 'flex', 'grid', 'padding'. Does this reduce CSS size?
options: Yes, disabling unused core plugins removes their utilities from the build
No, corePlugins only affects theme values, not utilities
Disabling plugins breaks Tailwind
All plugins must be enabled
explanation: corePlugins: false disables all default Tailwind plugins; selectively enabling only needed plugins (flex, grid, padding) reduces output CSS.

question: Your Tailwind build has layers: @tailwind base; @tailwind components; @tailwind utilities;. If the utilities layer is 40 KB and you add 10 small custom utilities with @layer utilities, does CSS size grow significantly?
options: No, @layer utilities adds to the utilities layer without major overhead if utilities are few; but 100 @layer utilities would bloat CSS
Yes, any @layer addition doubles CSS size
@layer doesn't affect final CSS size
Custom utilities always increase size
explanation: Adding a few custom utilities via @layer has minimal impact; but many custom utilities multiply CSS footprint; prefer Tailwind's utilities when possible.

question: A query runs in 5 seconds and examine 100,000 documents but returns only 10. What is the likely issue?
options: The query is poorly written and must be rewritten from scratch
The query examines too many documents relative to results (docsExamined >> nReturned); an index on the filter field would reduce examined documents
MongoDB is misconfigured for this workload
The 5-second latency is normal for this query complexity
explanation: High docsExamined/nReturned ratio indicates inefficient filtering; create an index on the filter field to reduce examined documents.

question: A collection has 10 indexes. Adding an 11th index is proposed. What is a downside?
options: Queries can only use one index, so more indexes don't help
Every insert/update/delete must update all 11 indexes, adding write overhead; unused indexes waste resources
MongoDB forbids more than 10 indexes
Index selection becomes random with >10 indexes
explanation: Each index adds write cost; maintain only necessary indexes; drop unused indexes to improve write performance.

question: Profiling is enabled at level 1. What does this capture?
options: All operations are profiled and logged
Only slow operations (> slowms threshold, default 100ms) are profiled and logged
Only index operations are profiled
Profile level 1 is not a valid setting
explanation: Profile level 1 logs operations exceeding the slowms threshold; level 0 disables profiling, level 2 logs all operations; useful for finding slow queries.

question: An explain() output shows stage: 'COLLSCAN'. What does this indicate?
options: The query used an index named COLLSCAN
A full collection scan was performed (no index used); queries on non-indexed fields use this inefficient stage
The query was optimized by MongoDB and is performing well
COLLSCAN is an error state; the query failed
explanation: COLLSCAN means no index was used; create an index on the filter field to avoid collection scans on large collections.

question: A connection pool is configured with minPoolSize: 10, maxPoolSize: 100. What does this control?
options: Document size limits
The minimum/maximum number of connections held to the database; too high uses memory, too low reduces concurrency
Query cache size
The pool size for replication connections only
explanation: Connection pools maintain persistent connections; minPoolSize keeps warm connections ready, maxPoolSize prevents resource exhaustion; balance for your workload.

question: An aggregation pipeline with $lookup on a 10M-document collection stalls. Memory usage spikes. What is likely?
options: $lookup is forbidden on large collections
$lookup loads unindexed joins into memory; an index on the foreignField would reduce memory usage and speed up the join
Aggregation pipelines have a hard memory limit of 1GB
The collection size is too large for aggregation
explanation: $lookup with unindexed join materializes results into memory; index the foreignField and localField to reduce memory and improve performance.

question: Batch inserts are performed: insertMany([doc1, doc2, ..., doc1000]). What is the advantage over individual insertOne() calls?
options: insertMany() is only marginally faster
insertMany() sends a single network round trip for all documents, reducing latency; individual inserts require 1000 round trips
insertMany() bypasses indexes; insertOne() enforces them
insertMany() supports only 100 documents per call
explanation: insertMany() batches requests, reducing round trips from N to 1; significant latency improvement for bulk inserts.

question: A query uses maxTimeMS: 5000. What happens if the query takes longer than 5 seconds?
options: The query continues; maxTimeMS is advisory
The query is terminated and a timeout error is returned
The client forcibly closes the connection
MongoDB pauses the query temporarily
explanation: maxTimeMS enforces a hard deadline; queries exceeding it are killed; useful for preventing long-running queries from blocking resources.

question: A read-heavy application uses readPreference: 'secondary' but experiences high latency. What is the issue?
options: Secondary reads are always slower than primary reads
Secondary nodes may have replication lag, returning stale data; with default secondary, reads hit any secondary, which may be slow or behind
Secondary queries don't use indexes
readPreference: 'secondary' is not a valid option
explanation: Secondaries vary in lag and performance; 'secondaryPreferred' with maxStalenessSeconds limits staleness; consider locality-aware read preference.

question: A large aggregation pipeline uses $group to aggregate 1M documents into 1000 results. Where does the bottleneck likely occur?
options: The $group stage reads 1M documents and aggregates; memory usage is proportional to group keys (1000); this is the bottleneck
The $match stage is always the bottleneck
Aggregation pipelines don't have bottlenecks
The network is the bottleneck
explanation: $group on 1M documents uses CPU and memory; optimize with $match early to reduce input before $group, or create an index on the group key.

question: A client sends 1000 individual GET commands sequentially. Each command has 1ms roundtrip latency. Total time is ~1000ms. Using pipelining, commands are batched in one request. What is the latency improvement?
options: No improvement; latency per command is unchanged
Reduces to ~1ms total; all commands in one roundtrip
Reduces to ~100ms; pipelining batches 10 per request
Depends on the network bandwidth
explanation: Pipelining sends all 1000 commands in one roundtrip, reducing total latency from 1000ms to ~1ms.

question: A Redis client maintains a connection pool of 10 connections. Each request checks out a connection, executes a command, and returns it. Is connection pooling beneficial if commands are pipelined?
options: No; pipelining obviates the need for pooling
Yes; pooling reduces per-command overhead
Depends; small batches benefit more from pooling
Yes; pooling prevents new-connection overhead on each request
explanation: Pooling reuses persistent connections; pipelining sends multiple commands per connection, maximizing efficiency.

question: You pipeline 100 commands, but one command returns an error. Does Redis continue processing the remaining commands?
options: No; pipeline aborts on first error
Yes; each command is processed independently; results buffer includes errors
Partially; commands after the error are skipped
Depends on the command type
explanation: Pipeline is fire-and-forget; all commands are queued and executed; errors are returned in the response array.

question: A key stores a 1MB JSON string. Accessing it via GET retrieves the entire 1MB over the network on every read. How can you optimize?
options: Split into Hashes; fetch only needed fields
Compress with GZIP; client decompresses
Use Streams with 100KB chunks
Reduce the TTL to minimize retrievals
explanation: Hashes allow selective field access; avoid transferring the entire 1MB if only a few fields are needed.

question: A Lua script increments 10 keys atomically. Without scripting, you would WATCH and MULTI/EXEC. Does Lua scripting reduce roundtrips?
options: No; Lua still requires individual commands
Yes; script runs server-side in one roundtrip
Depends on the script complexity
Lua reduces CPU but not network roundtrips
explanation: Lua scripts execute server-side; all commands run in a single roundtrip, reducing latency.

question: A sorted set has 1M members. ZRANGE to fetch the top 100 scores. Is this O(N) or O(log N)?
options: O(1) (cached)
O(log N) for range lookup
O(log N + K) where K is the range size (100)
O(N) (full scan)
explanation: ZRANGE is O(log N + K); the log N finds the start, then K elements are returned.

question: A hot key is accessed 10,000 times/sec by a single client. The client uses a single connection. Will multiple connections reduce latency?
options: No; single client throughput is bottlenecked by serialization
Yes; multiple connections parallelize requests
Depends; benefit is small for single-threaded clients
No; Redis is single-threaded; connections do not parallelize
explanation: Multiple connections allow a multi-threaded client to parallelize; single-threaded clients gain little benefit.

question: INFO stats shows evicted_keys increasing and hits dropping. What is the root cause, and how do you optimize?
options: Memory pressure is evicting keys; increase maxmemory or optimize key size
Client cache is misconfigured; no Redis issue
Network latency is causing timeouts; optimize routes
Replication lag is preventing cache updates; tune replication
explanation: Evictions and low hit rate indicate memory pressure; either grow the cache or reduce key sizes.

question: A client executes SCAN to iterate all keys. Each SCAN call takes 10ms. Iterating 1M keys takes ~1000s. Can SCAN be optimized?
options: No; SCAN is inherently slow
Yes; increase SCAN COUNT to batch more keys per call
Yes; use multiple SCAN cursors in parallel
Yes; switch to KEYS pattern (no blocking)
explanation: SCAN COUNT parameter controls batch size; larger COUNT returns more keys per roundtrip, reducing total time.

question: A sorted set ZRANGE query includes WITHSCORES, returning 200KB of scores. Scores are rarely needed. Should you store them?
options: Yes; scores are part of the sorted set definition
No; use a separate key for score lookups when needed
Store scores in a parallel Hash; avoid redundancy
Compress scores to reduce transfer size
explanation: If scores are rarely needed, omit WITHSCORES; query a separate score key on demand to reduce network traffic.

question: A JSON API re-serializes the same large static config on every request. What is the cheapest effective optimization?
options: Serialize it once and cache the resulting string
Switch from JSON.stringify to a for-loop
Add more CPU cores
Gzip the response with maximum compression level
explanation: If the payload is static, caching the pre-serialized string removes repeated CPU work on every request.

question: Under high concurrency, a hashing call using `crypto.pbkdf2Sync` degrades throughput. Why, and what helps?
options: The sync variant blocks the event loop; use the async crypto.pbkdf2 which offloads to the thread pool
pbkdf2 is insecure and should be removed
The salt is too long and slows hashing
Node caches hashes so repeated calls are free
explanation: Synchronous CPU-heavy crypto blocks the single event loop; the async API runs on libuv's thread pool, freeing the loop to handle other requests.

options: cache is freed automatically
cache grows infinitely, never freed
cache only stores recent entries
no memory leak exists
explanation: The cache object holds references indefinitely; cache grows unbounded as new IDs are requested, causing memory to grow until process crashes.

options: spawns one worker per CPU core, distributing requests
only one process runs regardless
clustering is deprecated
clustering slows down single requests
explanation: Multiple worker processes utilize all CPU cores; a master process distributes incoming requests, improving throughput on multi-core systems.

options: tells browsers to cache response for 1 hour
browsers cache on disk and reuse without new requests
improves server performance by reducing requests
all of the above
explanation: Cache-Control instructs browsers to store responses locally; subsequent requests within 1 hour skip the server, improving speed and reducing load.

options: profiling with perf_hooks identifies slow functions
guess which functions are slow
profiling is unnecessary
only production code is worth profiling
explanation: perf_hooks allows marking and measuring code execution time; profiling identifies which functions consume most time.

options: sends uncompressed file
compresses response body, reducing bandwidth
encryption replaces compression
gzip is deprecated
explanation: gzip compresses the response; browsers automatically decompress; bandwidth reduces by 60-80% for text, improving download speed.

options: creates new connection per query (slow)
reuses idle connections, avoiding connection creation overhead
pooling is optional
one connection per client
explanation: Creating connections is expensive; pooling maintains idle connections ready to reuse, eliminating handshake delays.

options: synchronous is simpler, avoid async
use async for I/O operations to not block event loop
sync and async have same performance
blocking is always preferred
explanation: I/O operations (file, network, database) should be async; blocking ties up the event loop, starving other requests.

question:
How does Node.js garbage collection (GC) affect performance?
```javascript
node --max-old-space-size=2048 app.js
```
options: GC pauses are unavoidable in all languages
GC pauses can cause latency spikes; tune heap size
larger heap = faster GC
GC is not relevant in Node.js
explanation: GC pauses stop execution; smaller heap = more frequent pauses; larger heap = longer pauses; tune to balance frequency vs. duration.

question: The slow query log shows a query taking 5 seconds. The query uses an index on the WHERE clause. What is the likely bottleneck?
options: The index is not being used; check EXPLAIN
Disk I/O reading the clustered index after index traversal
Sorting results in memory with filesort
Lock contention from concurrent transactions
explanation: Index lookup is fast; slowness often comes from clustered index (data) reads after the index narrows rows, especially with poor selectivity.

question: SHOW VARIABLES displays `innodb_buffer_pool_size = 1G` on a 8-core server with 16G RAM. The slow query log has 100+ entries daily. What allocation change improves performance?
options: Increase buffer_pool_size to 50% of RAM (8G) to cache more data
Decrease buffer_pool_size to free RAM for OS caching
Leave it unchanged; 1G is sufficient for most workloads
Increase to 100% of RAM (16G) to eliminate disk I/O entirely
explanation: Buffer pool caches frequently-accessed data; increasing to 8-10G (50-60% of RAM) reduces I/O, assuming queries are I/O-bound.

question: A table with 1M rows processes 10K INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements per second. The redo log fill rate is 500MB/s. What innodb_log_file_size is recommended?
options: 100MB (default); most workloads do not need large logs
500MB to match the fill rate and reduce checkpoint frequency
1GB to balance durability and checkpoint overhead
4GB to minimize I/O from checkpoint operations
explanation: Larger log files reduce checkpoint frequency; too small causes frequent checkpoints (I/O spikes); 1GB is a good starting point for heavy writes.

question: A query plan shows `Using temporary; Using filesort`. The result set is 100 rows. What optimization reduces these overheads?
options: Add an index on the ORDER BY columns to avoid filesort
Increase temp_table_size to keep the temporary table in memory
Reduce the number of DISTINCT columns to avoid temporary table creation
Use LIMIT to reduce the number of rows sorted
explanation: An index matching the GROUP BY/ORDER BY columns eliminates both temporary table and filesort; this is the most effective optimization.

question: SHOW PROCESSLIST shows a query with `State: Sending data` taking 30 seconds. The query returns 10M rows. What is happening?
options: The query is fetching rows from the clustered index; network I/O is slow
The query is blocked waiting for a lock; use SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS to confirm
The query is executing the ORDER BY clause; use LIMIT to reduce rows
The query is experiencing lock contention on the table
explanation: 'Sending data' means the server is reading and serializing result rows to send over the network—slow due to large result set size.

question: A table is queried frequently by year: `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE YEAR(created_at)=2026`. Performance degrades as data grows. What optimization is most effective?
options: Add a generated column YEAR(created_at) with an index on it
Rewrite the query to use range: `WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'`
Partition the table by YEAR(created_at) to enable partition pruning
Denormalize year into a separate year column and index it
explanation: Partitioning by year enables partition pruning; the query executor skips entire partitions, dramatically improving performance.

question: SHOW GLOBAL STATUS shows `Innodb_rows_read = 10M, Innodb_rows_updated = 1K`. The query update only targeted 1K rows but read 10M. What is the inefficiency?
options: The WHERE clause does not use an index; a full table scan reads 10M rows before filtering to 1K
The UPDATE uses a JOIN that scans a large table before matching 1K rows
The query is I/O-bound and reads pages multiple times
The storage engine performs extra validation scans
explanation: 10M rows read for 1K updates indicates poor WHERE selectivity—likely missing index or function-wrapped column prevents range scan.

question: A recurring ANALYZE TABLE statement is run nightly. What performance benefit does it provide?
options: Updates table statistics used by the query optimizer for join order and index selection
Defragments the table and reclaims unused disk space
Reorders rows for better I/O locality
Rebuilds all indexes to remove bloat
explanation: ANALYZE TABLE updates cardinality statistics; stale statistics lead to suboptimal plans, so regular runs improve query optimization.

question: Monitoring shows high `Innodb_buffer_pool_wait_free` counter. What is the consequence?
options: Threads are waiting for free buffer pool pages; the pool is too small or eviction is slow
Network I/O is saturated; bandwidth needs to be upgraded
Queries are executing slowly due to CPU contention
Replication lag is increasing because writes are stalled
explanation: High wait_free means the buffer pool is exhausted; threads block waiting for pages to be evicted—increase buffer_pool_size.

question: A stored procedure performs 1000 individual INSERT statements in a loop. Converting to multi-value INSERT `INSERT INTO t(...) VALUES (...), (...), ...` reduces execution from 10 seconds to 1 second. Why?
options: Multi-value INSERT reduces the number of parse/compile cycles
Each individual INSERT incurs lock overhead; multi-value batches reduce locking
Network round-trips are eliminated; one statement instead of 1000
The storage engine optimizes multi-value inserts with internal batching
explanation: Each INSERT is a network round-trip and context switch; multi-value reduces overhead from 1000 round-trips to 1.

question: PostgreSQL's shared_buffers is set to 256 MB on a 64 GB system. Queries are slow and disk I/O is high. What is the likely issue?
options: shared_buffers is too small; it should typically be 25% of system RAM; increasing it reduces disk I/O by keeping more data in cache
shared_buffers is too large
Disk I/O is unrelated to shared_buffers
shared_buffers cannot exceed 256 MB
explanation: shared_buffers is PostgreSQL's buffer pool; insufficient size causes repeated disk accesses for the same data; the rule of thumb is 25% of available RAM.

question: A server has 64 GB RAM and 32 CPU cores. work_mem is set to 4 MB. Sorting 10 million rows in a single query creates a temporary file on disk. Why does increasing work_mem help?
options: work_mem controls per-operation memory; increasing it allows sorts and aggregations to complete in memory rather than spilling to disk
work_mem limits total database memory
Sorts always use disk regardless of work_mem
work_mem is a per-connection limit and cannot be tuned globally
explanation: work_mem sets the per-operation limit for sorting, hashing, and aggregation; insufficient work_mem forces disk spillover, dramatically slowing queries.

question: A table with 100 million rows has autovacuum running, but dead tuples accumulate quickly. Queries on the table are slow. What parameters should be tuned?
options: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor and autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor control vacuum frequency; reducing them triggers more frequent vacuuming, clearing dead tuples faster
Autovacuum cannot be tuned
Vacuum should be run manually daily
Dead tuples do not affect query performance
explanation: Autovacuum parameters control vacuum thresholds; tables with high churn need aggressive tuning to prevent bloat and index degeneration.

question: A slow query is logged: `SELECT * FROM large_table LIMIT 100` runs for 5 seconds. EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan. What should be checked?
options: Whether log_min_duration_ms is set appropriately to log slow queries, and whether statistics are stale (run ANALYZE); stale stats may cause the planner to choose sequential scan
The LIMIT clause is broken
The table needs to be partitioned
Sequential scans are always fast
explanation: Stale statistics can cause poor planner decisions; log_min_duration_ms helps identify slow queries; ANALYZE recomputes statistics and may change plan selection.

question: A server runs hundreds of queries daily. Enabling query logging with log_statement = 'all' causes significant disk I/O overhead. What is a targeted alternative?
options: Use log_min_duration_ms to log only queries exceeding a threshold (e.g., 1000 ms), reducing overhead while capturing slow queries
Disable all logging
Query logging cannot be tuned
Use log_statement = 'mod' instead
explanation: Logging all queries is expensive; log_min_duration_ms logs only slow queries, balancing observability with performance.

question: A database experiences high CPU usage during business hours. Running `SELECT * FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_time DESC` shows a single query consuming 70% of CPU time. What should be done?
options: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to examine the query plan, identify bottlenecks (sequential scans, missing indexes, suboptimal joins), and optimize or create indexes as needed
The query runs in the application and cannot be optimized
CPU usage is normal
All queries should be equally fast
explanation: pg_stat_statements identifies top consumers; EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveals optimization opportunities like missing indexes or inefficient joins.

question: Connection count reaches the max_connections limit (default 100) and new connections are rejected. The application scales with more servers. What is the solution?
options: Use a connection pool (PgBouncer, Pgpool) to maintain fewer backend connections while serving many application clients, or increase max_connections with care
Increase max_connections indefinitely
Each application server should maintain its own connection to the database
PostgreSQL does not support connection pooling
explanation: Connection pooling multiplexes many client connections onto fewer database connections, reducing overhead and allowing horizontal scaling without overwhelming PostgreSQL.

question: A write-heavy workload has wal_buffers set to 16 MB. Disk I/O is high. Increasing wal_buffers to 256 MB does not help. What else should be checked?
options: Synchronous_commit controls WAL synchronization to disk; setting it to 'off' or 'local' reduces disk waits but sacrifices durability on server crash
wal_buffers is the only relevant tuning parameter
The storage device is healthy
Write performance is always I/O-bound
explanation: synchronous_commit trades durability for performance; 'off' writes asynchronously (faster but risky), 'local' waits for WAL flush to OS cache (safer and faster than disk sync).

question: A table grows by 10 GB monthly. After 2 years, full table scans take 30 minutes. Indexes are present and queries are well-optimized. Partitioning by date is considered. What benefit does partitioning provide?
options: Partition pruning excludes irrelevant partitions before scanning, reducing I/O and cache pressure; queries on recent data scan fewer partitions and run faster
Partitioning doubles query speed
Partitioning is only for sharding across servers
Partitioning slows queries
explanation: Partitioning enables the planner to eliminate entire partitions from queries, reducing scanned data and improving cache efficiency for time-series or large append-only tables.

question: An application uses connection pooling with 50 connections. Each connection sets custom configuration: `SET search_path TO myschema; SET work_mem TO '256 MB'`. This is done per query. What is the performance issue?
options: Repeatedly setting configurations has overhead; these should be set once per connection during pool initialization, not per query
Connections should change config per query
search_path affects query speed
work_mem cannot be set per connection
explanation: Configuration changes incur overhead; pooling benefits are lost if configuration is reset per query; set once at connection setup instead.

question: A query `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024` runs a full table scan despite an index on created_at. Why?
options: Wrapping the indexed column in a function prevents the index from being used
SELECT * always disables index usage
Indexes never work on date columns
The index must be rebuilt after every insert
explanation: Applying a function like YEAR() to an indexed column makes the predicate non-sargable, so the optimizer cannot use the index; a range condition on created_at would.

question:
A query takes 10 seconds. EXPLAIN PLAN shows:
Seq Scan on users (cost=0..5000 rows=1M)
with a predicate on status = 'active'.

What optimization would help?
options: Create an index on status to avoid the full table scan
Increase the table cache size
Rewrite the query using UNION
No optimization is possible
explanation: A full table scan (Seq Scan) on a 1M-row table is slow; an index on status enables efficient range access.

question:
A large table has stale statistics. EXPLAIN PLAN estimates rows incorrectly:
Index Scan cost=100 (estimated 1000 rows, actual 100k rows).

What causes the wrong estimate?
options: Outdated statistics from the last ANALYZE; rerun ANALYZE to update them
The index is broken
The query is written incorrectly
Incorrect statistics cannot be fixed
explanation: Query planners rely on statistics gathered by ANALYZE; outdated stats lead to poor plan choices; re-running ANALYZE fixes estimates.

question:
A query does a full table scan instead of using an available index. Why?
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount / 100 > 50;
options: Expression (amount/100) prevents index use; rewrite as amount > 5000 to use an index on amount
The index is always preferred; the planner should use it
Expressions never prevent index use
Full scans are faster for small result sets
explanation: Applying a function/expression to an indexed column disables index use; rewrite to apply the expression to the constant instead.

question:
A paginated query retrieves page 1000:
SELECT * FROM huge_table ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 OFFSET 99900;
options: OFFSET 99900 skips 99.9k rows (slow); use keyset pagination (WHERE id > last_id) instead
OFFSET is optimized for large values
Pagination has no performance impact
LIMIT always uses an index
explanation: Large OFFSET values require scanning and discarding many rows; keyset pagination (seek by last ID) avoids skipping.

options: Start with small_table, join to big_table (smaller set first reduces work)
Start with big_table, join to small_table
Join order doesn't matter; the optimizer chooses
Always join the larger table first
explanation: Joining the smaller table first (100 rows) against the larger one is more efficient than joining 10M rows against 100.

question:
Database memory is low. A query runs slow due to spilling to disk. How do you reduce memory usage?
SELECT DISTINCT name, COUNT(*) FROM huge_table GROUP BY name;
options: Add a LIMIT clause or use STREAMING GROUP BY if available to reduce memory footprint
Increase database memory allocation
Remove DISTINCT to speed up the query
Memory issues cannot be resolved in SQL
explanation: LIMIT reduces output rows; streaming aggregation processes groups incrementally; both reduce peak memory usage.

options: Rewrite using a window function: SELECT name FROM (SELECT *, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) avg_dept_salary FROM users) WHERE salary > avg_dept_salary
Remove the subquery entirely
Use a JOIN instead (though it's not semantically the same)
No optimization is possible
explanation: Window functions compute aggregates once per group instead of re-evaluating the subquery for each row.

question:
A query with many CASE WHEN conditions is slow:
SELECT id, CASE WHEN ... THEN ... WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END FROM big_table;
options: Complex expressions add CPU overhead; if many queries use the same logic, precompute in a lookup table
CASE is never optimized
Add an index to fix performance
Rewrite every CASE into a separate query
explanation: Many CASE branches add CPU cost; if used repeatedly, store pre-computed results in a table and JOIN instead.

options: Both; ANALYZE updates statistics and VACUUM reclaims space and defragments
Only ANALYZE helps
Only VACUUM helps
Neither operation helps
explanation: ANALYZE updates statistics for better planning; VACUUM removes dead tuples and defragments pages, improving cache efficiency.

question: Running `sleep 100 &` and then `kill -9 $!`, what is the immediate result?
options: The process is terminated immediately (SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored)
The process receives SIGKILL and gracefully shuts down
The process continues running (backgrounded processes ignore signals)
The shell waits for the process to handle the signal
explanation: SIGKILL (signal 9) is unconditional and immediately terminates any process; the process cannot catch it or perform cleanup.

question: After running `sleep 100 &` and `wait`, what happens if the sleep process hasn't terminated?
options: The shell waits for the background process to finish
The command times out after 30 seconds
The sleep process is forcibly killed
The shell returns immediately with an error
explanation: `wait` without arguments blocks the shell until all background jobs complete; if sleep is still running, wait will pause the prompt.

question: A process appears in `ps aux` as `<defunct>`. What state is it in?
options: Zombie process (terminated but parent hasn't reaped it via wait)
Process in uninterruptible sleep (D state)
Process that voluntarily exited but still holds resources
Process waiting for a signal from the parent
explanation: A zombie is a process that exited but whose parent hasn't called `wait()` to retrieve its exit status; the kernel keeps a minimal entry until reaped.

question: Running `bash -c 'sleep 100' &` and then the parent bash exits without `wait`. What happens to sleep?
options: Sleep is reparented to init/systemd and continues running (orphaned process adoption)
Sleep is killed automatically
Sleep becomes a zombie
Sleep is paused until the parent returns
explanation: When a process's parent exits, the kernel reparents it to PID 1 (init/systemd); the orphaned process keeps running and is reaped when it exits.

question: What is the difference between `kill -15` and `kill -9` in terms of cleanup?
options: SIGTERM (-15) can be caught to clean up; SIGKILL (-9) terminates immediately without cleanup
SIGTERM waits 5 seconds for cleanup; SIGKILL waits 10 seconds
Both allow the same cleanup; SIGKILL is just faster
SIGTERM only works on interactive processes
explanation: SIGTERM (15) is a polite termination request the process can catch to close files/connections; SIGKILL (9) is unconditional and allows no cleanup.

question: Running `ps aux | grep sleep`, what is the PIDs relationship between the grep process and the sleep process shown?
options: Unrelated; grep is a separate process that searches /proc and shows matching lines
Grep is the parent of sleep
Sleep and grep share the same PID
Grep adopts sleep's PID after printing
explanation: Grep reads the output of `ps aux` (which lists all processes in a snapshot) and filters lines; it's unrelated to the sleep process's lifecycle.

question: A process has PPID=1. What does this indicate?
options: The parent process is init/systemd (usually means the original parent exited)
The process is the first user-space process
The process is a kernel thread
The process is running at init-level priority
explanation: PPID 1 means the parent process ID is 1, typically init or systemd; this usually happens when a process is orphaned.

question: Running `( sleep 100 & ); kill %1` in the shell, what happens?
options: Job %1 is not found (the subshell ends; job is no longer tracked by the parent shell)
The sleep process is killed
The subshell is killed instead of sleep
Kill waits for sleep to exit first
explanation: The subshell in parentheses creates a new shell context; backgrounding sleep there adds it to the subshell's job list, which is lost when the subshell exits.

question: What does `strace -p $PID` accomplish?
options: Attaches to a running process and traces all system calls it makes (useful for debugging)
Starts tracing and runs a new command
Lists all processes matching the pattern
Prints stack traces for a process
explanation: `strace -p` attaches to an existing process and logs every system call, showing what the process is doing at the kernel level.

question: A process is in state `S` when shown by `ps aux`. What does this indicate?
options: Sleeping interruptibly (waiting for I/O or an event; responsive to signals)
Stopped by a signal (SIGSTOP)
Suspended (similar to stopped)
Synchronized (waiting for a lock)
explanation: `S` state (capital S) means interruptible sleep; the process is waiting but can be woken by signals; lowercase `s` is different (session leader).

question:
A production server has DEBUG=True and the admin interface is accessible. What is the security risk?

```python
# settings.py
DEBUG = True
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*']
```
options: DEBUG=True exposes sensitive data (settings, source code) in error pages
The admin interface is secure; DEBUG mode does not affect it
ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] prevents access from unauthorized hosts
DEBUG=True only affects development servers, not production
explanation: DEBUG=True exposes SECRET_KEY, database queries, source code, and settings in error pages; set DEBUG=False and ALLOWED_HOSTS properly in production.

question:
A static files collection is run in production but some files are missing. What is the cause?

```bash
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
# Some CSS files are not in staticfiles/ directory
```
options: STATIC_ROOT or STATIC_URL is misconfigured; check settings.py
Third-party app static files are excluded by default
CSS files must be in STATICFILES_DIRS; app static folders are ignored
A custom storage backend is required to collect static files
explanation: Check STATIC_ROOT (destination) and STATIC_URL (URL path) settings; also verify staticfiles is in INSTALLED_APPS and apps have a static/ folder with correct structure.

question:
A production database connection uses DATABASE_URL but the URL is exposed in the Heroku config. Is this a security issue?

```python
import dj_database_url
DATABASES['default'] = dj_database_url.config()
```
options: Yes, DATABASE_URL in env vars can be logged or leaked
No, environment variables are secure in production platforms
Depends on the database provider's security settings
DATABASE_URL is automatically encrypted by dj_database_url
explanation: Environment variables can be logged, leaked in error pages, or exposed in configs; use a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) for sensitive credentials.

question:
A production server runs Django via Gunicorn but static files return 404. Why?

```bash
gunicorn myapp.wsgi:application
# Static files (CSS, JS) return 404
```
options: Gunicorn does not serve static files; use a reverse proxy (Nginx) or WhiteNoise
STATIC_ROOT must point to a directory accessible by Gunicorn
The web server must run collectstatic before Gunicorn starts
A WSGI middleware is needed to serve static files
explanation: Gunicorn is a WSGI server and does not serve static files; use Nginx/Apache as a reverse proxy or WhiteNoise middleware to serve static files.

question:
A migration fails in production with a data migration. What is the safest approach?

```bash
python manage.py migrate --plan  # Review before applying
python manage.py migrate         # May take time or fail
```
options: Back up the database before running migrations
Test the migration on a staging database first
Run collectstatic before migration to avoid conflicts
Both A and B are necessary precautions
explanation: Always back up production data and test migrations in staging before production; verify with --plan and monitor execution.

question:
A production server uses a custom Middleware but it is not registered. Why is it not executed?

```python
# settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'myapp.middleware.CustomMiddleware',  # Wrong path?
]
```
options: The middleware is ignored; it must inherit from MiddlewareMixin
The string path must resolve to the middleware class; verify the import path
Middleware is loaded at startup; changes require a server restart
Custom middleware requires explicit registration in urls.py
explanation: Check the middleware import path; it must resolve to a class; test with `python -c 'from myapp.middleware import CustomMiddleware'`.

question:
A production load balancer routes requests to multiple Django instances. What is a session consistency issue?

```
Request 1 (instance A): user.session['id'] = 123
Request 2 (instance B): user.session['id'] = ?  # Missing if sessions not shared
```
options: Sessions are stored in a shared database or cache, so instance B sees the session
Each instance has its own session storage; session data is lost on different instance
Load balancer ensures all requests go to the same instance
SESSION_ENGINE setting handles session sharing automatically
explanation: Without shared session storage (database or Redis), each instance has separate session data; use a shared backend (cache_db) to ensure consistency.

question:
A background task is queued using Celery but tasks are not being executed. What is the issue?

```python
from celery import shared_task

@shared_task
def send_email(user_id):
    # Task code
    pass

send_email.delay(123)  # Task is queued but not executed
```
options: The Celery worker process is not running
The task is queued but the worker does not have the task code
Celery requires BROKER_URL to be configured in settings
All of the above are possible causes
explanation: Check: (1) Celery worker is running, (2) BROKER_URL and result backend are configured, (3) Worker has loaded the task module, (4) INSTALLED_APPS includes 'celery'.

options: DummyCache disables caching; all cache.get() calls return None
DummyCache falls back to database caching automatically
The site works but is slower because nothing is cached
DummyCache is safe for production; it prevents cache stampedes
explanation: DummyCache is a null backend that disables caching (used for testing); in production, use Redis or Memcached for actual caching.

options: No risk; the check confirms the system is working
High risk; load balancers query health endpoints frequently, overloading the database
Risk only if the database is slow; fast queries are safe
Health checks should never access the database
explanation: Frequent health check queries can overload the database; use a simple response (e.g., HTTP 200) without queries, or cache the result with a short TTL.

question: You build a Vue app with `npm run build` for production. The build output includes a .js.map file. Should you deploy the source maps?
options: Yes, source maps are necessary for debugging; always deploy them
No, source maps expose source code; disable them in production or restrict server-side access with authentication
Only deploy source maps if you have a Sentry or error tracking account
Source maps are removed automatically in production builds; you cannot deploy them
explanation: Source maps reveal code; either disable them (set devtool: false) or restrict access server-side; use error tracking services instead.

question: Your production build uses `process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'`. At build time, what value is set?
options: NODE_ENV is set by the bundler; Vite and Webpack set it to 'production' during npm run build
NODE_ENV is a runtime value and is not available at build time
You must set NODE_ENV=production npm run build explicitly
NODE_ENV is only set in .env files; bundlers do not automatically set it
explanation: Bundlers automatically set NODE_ENV to 'production' during builds; build tools use this for optimizations and dead code elimination.

question: Your app loads large JavaScript chunks dynamically. How do you ensure users download the latest version after a deploy?
options: Versioned chunk filenames ensure cache busting; old users get new code
Set Cache-Control headers with short TTL; chunk names are hashed, so new versions have different names
Use a service worker to check for updates on every load
Manual cache clearing is the only reliable method
explanation: Bundlers generate hashed filenames; new code has different hashes, forcing browsers to re-download; set short Cache-Control TTL for index.html.

question: A critical bug is found in production. The current version is 2.1.0 and the fix is in a hotfix branch. What is the recommended rollback strategy?
options: Revert the broken commit and redeploy from main
Deploy the hotfix branch immediately; it is faster than reverting the commit
Redeploy the previous successful build (2.0.0) while the hotfix is tested in parallel
Wait for a full release cycle; hotfixes are too risky for immediate deployment
explanation: Immediate rollback to a known-good version is safest; test the hotfix in parallel and deploy it when ready.

question: Your app crashes on load with an error. The error tracking service shows it is a hydration mismatch in a third-party library. Can you safely ignore it?
options: Yes, hydration mismatches are harmless and do not affect functionality
No, Vue discards the server HTML and re-renders, defeating SSR benefits and causing layout shift
Only if the error happens in a non-critical component
Hydration mismatches are a development-only warning; they do not occur in production
explanation: Hydration mismatches cause Vue to discard server HTML and re-render, losing performance; investigate and fix the mismatch.

question: You want to analyze bundle size in production to find what is using the most space. What is the best tool?
