explanation: The HTTP Content-Type header (e.g., `text/html; charset=utf-8`) is read before the HTML parser starts, so the parser uses server-declared encoding from the beginning.

question: A document has `<html lang='en-US'>` but client JavaScript sets `document.documentElement.lang = 'es'`. Which language do screen readers announce?
options: en-US because the html attribute is the source of truth
es because javascript dynamically updates the attribute
the browser caches en-US and ignores the change
es only if the change occurs before the page fully loads
explanation: Assistive tech monitors live DOM attributes; updating `lang` dynamically with JavaScript changes the announced language immediately.

question: An HTML file is missing `<!DOCTYPE html>`. The page renders in quirks mode. Which rendering behavior is likely?
options: box model uses content-box instead of border-box
older browsers apply non-standard css interpretation
modern browsers reset doctype assumption and revert to standards mode
the page renders identically to a proper doctype
explanation: Quirks mode activates legacy rendering behaviors to support old websites; modern browsers interpret older CSS rules and may differ from standards mode in box sizing, margins, and padding.

question: A document declares `<html lang='en-US'>` but has no `<head>`. Where do CSS and JavaScript loads go?
options: the browser auto-inserts a head element for them
css and js fail to load because head is required
they are parsed as part of body and loaded in order
the browser rejects the document as malformed
explanation: HTML5 parsers auto-insert missing structural elements (`<head>`, `<body>`) to maintain valid tree structure, so CSS/JS in `<body>` are moved to the inserted `<head>`.

question: Why might `<meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width'>` fail on a page served with `<meta http-equiv='X-UA-Compatible' content='IE=5'>`?
options: the x-ua-compatible meta forces internet explorer 5 rendering, ignoring viewport
both metas conflict and only the first one is applied
viewport only works if x-ua-compatible is absent
the x-ua-compatible meta is deprecated and causes parsing errors
explanation: The `X-UA-Compatible` header/meta forces a specific IE rendering mode, which takes precedence; if it targets IE5, modern viewport scaling is disabled.

question: A document has `<meta http-equiv='refresh' content='5; url=http://example.com'>`. Which statement is true?
options: the page redirects after 5 seconds without server involvement
redirect only works if the server sends a matching refresh header
meta refresh is ignored by modern browsers for security
meta refresh only works if placed before meta charset
explanation: The meta refresh directive causes the browser to navigate after the specified delay; it is a client-side redirect that works independently of server headers.

question: A page loads `<link rel='stylesheet' href='style.css'>` in head and `<link rel='stylesheet' href='style.css'>` again in body. How many HTTP requests are made?
options: two requests, one for each link tag
one request with caching preventing the second
one request because the browser deduplicates identical links
varies by browser implementation
explanation: Modern browsers cache fetched resources by URL; if the browser fetches the CSS on the first link, the second link request is served from the browser cache without a network round-trip.

question: A document has `<noscript>JavaScript is disabled</noscript>` in the head. When does this appear?
options: only if javascript is disabled at the browser setting level
only if a script tag fails to load or errors
if javascript is not supported or explicitly disabled
noscript only works in body, not in head
explanation: The `<noscript>` element displays its content when the browser does not support JavaScript or when JavaScript is disabled; placement in head is valid and displays before body renders.

question: Why might a page with `<base href='https://example.com/docs/'>` and `<a href='intro.html'>` navigate to an unexpected URL?
options: relative hrefs are resolved against the base, resulting in https://example.com/docs/intro.html
the base element applies only to forms, not anchor links
anchor href ignores base and always uses the current page path
the browser invalidates the href due to base conflicting with the domain
explanation: The `<base>` element sets the base URL for resolving all relative URLs in the document, so `intro.html` becomes `https://example.com/docs/intro.html`.

question: A document has `<head><script src='app.js'></script></head><body>...</body>`. The page is blank until the script finishes loading. Why?
options: script tags in head block html parsing until the script runs
the script must run before the dom is available
browser waits for head to complete before rendering body
an error in the script is preventing body from rendering
explanation: By default, `<script>` tags are render-blocking; the HTML parser pauses while the script loads and executes, delaying initial render until the script completes.

question: A script uses `element.innerHTML = ''`. What security vulnerability is this?
options: innerHTML parses html and executes event handlers, creating an xss vulnerability
innerHTML is safe because it escapes html
onerror attributes are not executed in innerHTML context
the script is invalid and causes an error
explanation: innerHTML parses HTML markup, including event handlers; user-controlled HTML injected via innerHTML can execute arbitrary JavaScript (XSS).

question: A script uses `element.textContent = 'Bold'`. What displays in the element?
options: the text 'Bold' is displayed literally
bold text is rendered and displayed
an error occurs because textcontent does not accept html
the element remains empty
explanation: textContent treats its input as plain text, not HTML; angle brackets and tags are displayed as literal characters, not parsed as markup.

question: A script finds an element with `document.querySelector('#main .widget')`. If no element matches, what is returned?
options: null is returned if no match is found
an empty array is returned
undefined is returned
a nodelist with zero items is returned
explanation: querySelector returns the first matching element or null if no match is found; querySelectorAll returns a NodeList (possibly empty).

question: A script uses `parent.appendChild(child)`. If child already exists elsewhere in the DOM, what happens?
options: child is cloned and appended, leaving the original in place
the child is moved from its current location to the parent
an error occurs because child is already in the tree
child appears in both locations
explanation: appendChild removes the child from its current location and reinserts it at the new position; a node cannot exist in two places simultaneously.

question: A script uses `element.addEventListener('click', handler, true)`. What does the third parameter do?
options: true enables event bubbling
true enables event capturing (fire during capture phase)
true removes the listener after firing once
the third parameter is ignored in modern browsers
explanation: The third parameter (useCapture) determines if the listener fires during the capture phase (true) or bubbling phase (false, default).

question: A script uses `element.removeEventListener('click', namedFunction)`. If namedFunction was added with an arrow function instead, what happens?
options: the event listener is removed successfully
the removal fails because arrow functions cannot be removed
arrow functions are removed but named functions persist
removeEventListener does not distinguish between function types
explanation: removeEventListener requires the exact same function reference; if added with an inline or arrow function without storing a reference, removal will fail.

question: A script inserts `<script>alert('loaded')</script>` via innerHTML. Does the script execute?
options: the script executes immediately
the script is parsed but not executed
scripts inserted via innerHTML are executed asynchronously
scripts inserted via innerHTML never execute
explanation: Scripts inserted via innerHTML are parsed as text content and are not executed; they are inert and must be inserted via appendChild or eval (not recommended).

question: A script uses `element.getAttribute('data-value')` vs `element.dataset.value`. Which returns the live attribute value?
options: getAttribute always returns the current attribute value from the dom
dataset reflects attribute changes in real time
both always return the current value
getAttribute caches the value, dataset does not
explanation: getAttribute reads the current HTML attribute directly; dataset is a convenient accessor but both reflect live attribute values.

question: A script uses `element.parentElement` vs `element.parentNode`. On an element with no parent, what is the difference?
options: parentElement returns null, parentNode returns undefined
both return null
parentElement returns the document, parentnode returns null
there is no difference
explanation: Both parentElement and parentNode return null if there is no parent; the difference is that parentNode can be a text node, while parentElement is always an element.

question: A script uses `element.cloneNode(true)` to duplicate a subtree. Event listeners attached to the original are cloned with it?
options: event listeners are cloned and remain attached
event listeners are not cloned; only the dom structure is
clonenode copies listeners only if they were added with addeventlistener
cloning listeners depends on the browser
explanation: cloneNode duplicates the DOM tree structure only; event listeners attached via JavaScript are not cloned.

question: A form has `<input type='email' name='email'>` but the field is not submitted. Why might the name attribute be missing?
options: input without name is not submitted because the form has no reference to it
input without name is submitted with a default name
the type email prevents submission
missing name causes a form validation error
explanation: Form controls without a `name` attribute are excluded from form submission; the browser pairs `name` with the value to create the form data.

question: A form uses `<input type='submit' value='Send'>` and `<input type='reset'>`. The reset button appears blank. Why?
options: reset type does not support value attribute
reset requires an explicit value to display text
the value is set via label instead of the value attribute
reset input is not rendered
explanation: The `<input type='reset'>` without a `value` attribute displays a default localized label (e.g., 'Reset'); to customize, set an explicit `value`.

question: A form field is defined as `<input type='text' value='placeholder'><label>Enter name</label>`. Why is this an accessibility issue?
options: value and placeholder should not both be used
label must come before input in the html
the value is confused with user input; placeholder should be used instead
label is not associated with the input via for and id
explanation: A label without an explicit association (via `for` and `id`) is not semantically linked to the input, breaking accessibility for screen readers.

question: A form has `<form method='GET'><input type='password' name='pwd'></form>`. Why is this a security issue?
options: get method sends data in the url query string, exposing the password
password fields cannot be used with get
the form is invalid without a submit button
password data is always encrypted regardless of method
explanation: GET method appends form data to the URL, making passwords visible in browser history, logs, and referrer headers; POST with HTTPS is required for sensitive data.

question: A form has `<fieldset disabled><input type='text' name='field'></fieldset>`. When submitted, what value is sent?
options: the field value is sent normally
disabled fieldset disables all children, so no value is sent
an empty string is sent for the disabled field
the form submission is blocked entirely
explanation: A disabled `<fieldset>` disables all form controls within it; disabled controls are excluded from form submission.

question: A form uses `<input type='checkbox' name='agree' value='yes'>`. If unchecked and submitted, what is sent?
options: value='yes' is sent because the input has a value
nothing is sent because unchecked checkboxes are excluded
an empty value is sent for the checkbox
name='agree' is sent with no value
explanation: Unchecked checkboxes are not included in form submission at all; only checked checkboxes send their `name` and `value` pair.

question: A form has two submit buttons: `<button type='submit' name='action' value='save'>Save</button>` and `<button type='submit' name='action' value='draft'>Draft</button>`. Which button's value is submitted?
options: both button values are submitted
only the first button's value is submitted
the button that was clicked submits its value
buttons without value attribute are not submitted
explanation: When a form has multiple submit buttons, only the clicked button's `name` and `value` are included in form submission.

question: A form uses `<input type='email' required>`. The user submits empty. What happens?
options: the form is submitted with an empty email field
the browser blocks submission and shows a validation message
javascript validation is triggered
the server receives the submission and validates
explanation: HTML5 form validation (`required`, `type`, etc.) is enforced by the browser; empty required fields trigger a validation error before submission.

question: A form uses `<input type='text' inputmode='numeric'>`. Why might this not enforce numeric-only input?
options: inputmode is a hint for on-screen keyboards and does not prevent non-numeric input
inputmode is deprecated
type='text' overrides inputmode
browsers ignore inputmode on desktop
explanation: The `inputmode` attribute hints to mobile keyboards to show a numeric layout, but does not prevent non-numeric characters; `type='number'` enforces numeric validation.

question: A form field uses `<input type='text' maxlength='5'>`. A user pastes '123456'. What is submitted?
options: the entire pasted text '123456' is submitted because maxlength does not apply to paste
only the first 5 characters '12345' are submitted
the paste is rejected and the original field value is preserved
behavior varies by browser
explanation: The `maxlength` attribute limits input length regardless of paste operations; pasted text is truncated to the maximum length.

question:
A page has `

Welcome

` as the first visible heading, with no h1. Why might this confuse the document outline?
options: the outline starts with h2 instead of h1, creating an implicit h1 at the top level
h1 is required and the page is invalid without it
screen readers skip h2 if h1 is missing
the outline is unaffected, h2 as the first heading is valid
explanation: The HTML5 outline algorithm creates an implicit untitled section if the first heading is not h1; this breaks logical hierarchy for assistive tech users.

question: A page has two `<h1>` tags: one in header and one in main. Why is this problematic for SEO?
options: search engines penalize pages with multiple h1 tags
the first h1 is treated as the page title, the second confuses ranking
multiple h1s indicate missing page hierarchy to crawlers
modern search engines handle multiple h1s correctly and rank normally
explanation: While modern search engines are more forgiving, multiple h1 tags historically confused outline algorithms and hierarchy signals; best practice is one h1 per page for clarity.

question: A page skips from `<h1>` to `<h3>` with no h2 between them. A screen reader user navigates by headings. What happens?
options: the screen reader announces a missing h2 level
the outline shows h3 nested under h1 with an implied h2
navigation continues normally; h2 omission is ignored
the page structure is invalid and rendering stops
explanation: The HTML5 outline algorithm creates implicit heading levels for skipped hierarchy, so h3 becomes nested under h1, which may confuse navigation.

question: A developer uses `<h4>` for a prominent page title and `<h1>` for small component labels. Why is this backwards?
options: h1 should be the primary page title, h4 should be smaller subsections
headings are purely semantic and can be used in any order
h4 is deprecated and cannot be used for titles
css styling makes hierarchy irrelevant
explanation: Heading levels indicate semantic importance and document structure; h1 should mark the main page title, h4 should mark deeper subsections, regardless of visual size.

question:
Why might `

Page Title

` plus a visible h2 break accessibility?
options: hidden h1 is still in the outline, creating a mismatch with visible h2
display:none removes the element from the dom and outline
screen readers ignore display:none elements
visibility:hidden would work better than display:none
explanation: Even with `display:none`, the h1 exists in the DOM and outline, so screen readers see an h1-to-h2 jump while sighted users only see h2, causing confusion.

question:
A page has `

Widgets

` in the header, then later `

Widgets

` in the footer. Which is true?
options: html5 allows this; both are treated as separate page titles
search engines count both h1s and may lower ranking
the second h1 starts a new implicit section in the outline
duplicate h1 text is invalid and one must be removed
explanation: In HTML5 outline algorithm, each h1 starts a new implicit section; multiple h1s with the same text typically indicate missing structure rather than proper hierarchy.

question:
A `

options: hgroup suppresses h2 from the outline, treating both as a single heading unit
hgroup is deprecated and should not be used
hgroup only works if h1 comes after h2
the outline shows h1 and h2 separately regardless of hgroup
explanation: `<hgroup>` is designed to group related headings so that only the h1 enters the outline, suppressing the h2 subtitle from hierarchy navigation.

question:
A page uses `

Important Section

` inside a reusable component. When the component is embedded twice, why might the outline break?
options: the h2 is repeated, creating duplicate headings in the outline
components should only use h6 to avoid hierarchy conflicts
the outline algorithm nests the second h2 differently than the first
component headings must be dynamic based on nesting depth
explanation: Outline algorithm nesting is context-dependent; the same h2 in different parts of the page may nest at different levels, breaking consistent hierarchy.

question:
A developer marks up `

Bold Title

`. Does the strong tag affect heading semantics?
options: strong inside h1 changes the semantic level of the heading
heading semantics are unchanged; strong is just styling
strong suppresses the h1 from the outline
strong forces the heading to be treated as h2
explanation: Inline elements like `<strong>` do not change heading semantics; the heading level is determined by the h1-h6 tag, not its children.

question: Why is using a heading tag for styling (e.g., `<h6>` because it is the smallest) considered an anti-pattern?
options: heading tags must match visual size or the page is invalid
using heading for style violates semantic html; css should control size
h6 is deprecated and should never be used
screen readers announce h6 differently, confusing users
explanation: Heading semantics should reflect document structure, not visual presentation; CSS controls size, so using h1-h6 for styling alone disconnects semantics from outline.

question: A browser parser encounters `<br clear="left">`. Why does this fail to clear in modern HTML?
options: the clear attribute is deprecated and deprecated attributes are ignored
br is a void element and cannot accept non-boolean attributes
html5 deprecated clear in favor of css floats
the value left is invalid for non-block elements
explanation: HTML5 removed the clear attribute as a presentation concern; clearing floats is now purely a CSS responsibility.

question: A form field is defined as `<input name='password' disabled>`. Which statement is true about form submission?
options: the field is submitted with an empty string value
the field is omitted from submission entirely
the field is submitted with the name attribute only
submission is prevented by the disabled attribute
explanation: Disabled form controls are excluded from form submission regardless of whether they have a value.

question: Given `<meta charset="UTF-8">` placed after `<title>`, a page displays mojibake (garbled characters). What is the root cause?
options: utf-8 encoding is incompatible with the title element
charset meta must appear before any content including title
the server sent an incorrect content-type header
the browser has cached incorrect encoding detection
explanation: The charset meta tag must appear in the first 1024 bytes of the document head before any content to ensure the parser uses correct encoding from the start.

question: Why does `<input type='email' value='test@example.com' readonly>` differ from `<input type='email' value='test@example.com' disabled>`?
options: readonly still allows javascript to modify the value, disabled does not
readonly is submitted in forms, disabled is excluded
readonly allows keyboard focus, disabled does not
readonly appears as editable to screen readers, disabled does not
explanation: Readonly fields are included in form submission (readonly data is sent), but disabled fields are completely excluded.

question:
A single page has `

Product

` twice and uses entity-encoded `<h2>Subtitle</h2>` for display. Which breaks accessibility?
options: entity-encoded tags are parsed as text and assistive tech sees them
two h1 elements confuse screen readers into skipping the second one
entities are always parsed visually so markup intent is lost
headings encoded as entities bypass outline algorithms
explanation: Entity-encoded HTML markup (`<h1>`) is rendered as literal text, not parsed as an element, so it is invisible to accessibility tree algorithms and SEO parsers.

question: An SVG is embedded as `<svg><defs><style>circle{fill:red}</style></defs><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40'/></svg>`. The circle appears green, not red. Why?
options: svg does not support inline styles inside defs
the circle element is defined before the style rule applies
external css is overriding the embedded style
svgs require xlink namespace for style application
explanation: External CSS rules (from the page's stylesheets) have higher specificity than styles defined inside SVG `<defs>`, so page-level styles override embedded SVG styles.

question: Which void element must NOT have a closing tag in HTML5?
options: img
br
hr
all of the above are valid void elements
explanation: All three (img, br, hr) are void elements in HTML5; they never have closing tags and never wrap content.

question: A developer writes `<div data-count='5'>` and later reads `element.getAttribute('data-count')` returning `'5'`, but `element.dataset.count` returns `5`. Which statement is true?
options: getattribute returns a number, dataset returns a string
dataset auto-converts numeric strings to numbers
getattribute reads the raw html, dataset applies type coercion
this is browser-dependent and will fail in some environments
explanation: getAttribute() returns the raw HTML string value; the dataset API parses data-* attributes and may coerce types, but both ultimately return strings in conformant implementations.

question: An HTML5 document has `<!DOCTYPE html>` but the page serves as `application/xhtml+xml`. Which parsing mode activates?
options: html5 mode because doctype always determines parsing
xhtml strict mode because content-type overrides doctype
html5 mode unless the content-type is explicitly set
parser defaults to quirks mode due to conflicting signals
explanation: When the Content-Type header explicitly specifies `application/xhtml+xml`, the browser uses XML parsing mode regardless of the HTML5 DOCTYPE, requiring valid XML structure.

question: Why might `<a href='#section' id='section'>` create a navigation loop issue on some browsers?
options: the id matches the href, causing infinite history entries when clicked
anchor ids must be unique, and href references create duplicate ids
browsers treat self-referential anchors as page reloads
focus management directs to the element, then immediately back to the link
explanation: Clicking an anchor that links to itself can cause browsers to add redundant history entries or create navigation loops in some implementations.

question: A page uses `<canvas id='draw'></canvas>`. The canvas appears blank. What is likely missing?
options: canvas requires a specific doctype to render
javascript is needed to draw on the canvas
canvas must have a src attribute pointing to an image
canvas needs a width and height in the html
explanation: Canvas is rendered as an empty element by default; JavaScript is required to get the context and draw content using methods like `fillRect()` or `strokePath()`.

question: A page stores `<script type='application/json' id='data'>{"users": []}</script>`. Why is this a valid data storage technique?
options: script tags with type='application/json' are parsed as data, not code
the browser ignores the script tag but stores the content for js access
json inside script tags is not executed and is accessible via textContent
this technique is deprecated and should not be used
explanation: A `<script>` tag with a non-JavaScript type (like `application/json`) is not executed; JavaScript can parse its `textContent` to access embedded data.

question: A video uses `<video><source src='video.mp4'><track kind='subtitles' src='subs.vtt'></video>`. What is the track element used for?
options: track adds subtitles or captions that display over the video
track specifies alternative video formats
track adds chapter markers to the video
track defines video metadata
explanation: The `<track>` element adds text-based content like subtitles, captions, descriptions, or chapters to a `<video>` element, sourced from a WebVTT or similar file.

question: A page uses `<input type='number' min='1' max='10' step='0.5'>`. A user enters '5'. What is the outcome?
options: the value 5 is accepted because it is between 1 and 10
the value is rejected because 5 is not a valid step
the browser adjusts the value to the nearest step
the input requires a decimal value like 5.0
explanation: The `step` attribute defines valid increments (e.g., 0.5, 1, 2), but browsers typically accept any valid number between min and max, then constrain on submission if needed.

question: A page uses `<meter value='6' min='0' max='10'></meter>`. What does the meter element display?
options: a horizontal bar indicating progress at 60%
a gauge or measurement indicator at 6 out of 10
the percentage value as text
the meter element is decorative and requires css to display
explanation: The `<meter>` element displays a gauge-like visual representation of a measurement within a range (not progress); it shows the proportion of value within min/max.

question: A page uses `<progress value='50' max='100'></progress>`. Why might the progress bar not show on some browsers?
options: progress requires a width style to be visible
some browsers render progress as text instead of a visual bar
progress is a newer html5 element with limited support
progress bar styling varies by browser, but it should render visually
explanation: Modern browsers render `<progress>` as a visual bar; styling and appearance vary (some may show as a simple rectangle), but the element should display on all current browsers.

question: A page uses `<output>5</output>` and updates it via JavaScript to `10`. What is the output element's purpose?
options: output displays calculated or user-input results without form submission
output is a generic container like div
output requires form wrapping to be valid
output is semantically identical to a span
explanation: The `<output>` element represents the result of a calculation or user interaction; it is semantically meaningful for assistive tech to recognize as a result area.

question: A page uses `<input type='color' value='#FF0000'>`. What picker is displayed?
options: a text input for entering hex color codes
a native color picker dialog or widget
a dropdown list of web colors
the color type is not supported and displays as text input
explanation: The `type='color'` input displays a native color picker (appearance varies by browser); users can select or input color values, which are returned as hex strings.

question: A page uses `<time datetime='2024-07-22T15:30:00Z'>3:30 PM</time>`. Why is the datetime attribute useful?
options: it allows screen readers to announce the date/time accurately
it helps search engines and assistive tech parse the date semantically
it changes how the date is displayed visually
it enables browser-based event scheduling
explanation: The `datetime` attribute in ISO 8601 format allows machines (search engines, assistive tech, calendar apps) to parse the date unambiguously, while the text content is human-readable.

question: A page uses `<embed src='plugin.swf'>` for Flash. On modern browsers without Flash, what displays?
options: a broken plugin icon
nothing is displayed
fallback html inside embed is shown
embed requires a type attribute or it is invalid
explanation: The `<embed>` element is a self-closing void element with no fallback content support; if the plugin is not available, a broken/missing icon typically displays.

question: An image uses ``. Why might this pass WCAG without describing the image?
options: empty alt text is invalid and will fail all accessibility checks
alt='' marks the image as decorative and is skipped by screen readers
empty alt requires a figure element with figcaption instead
screen readers substitute the filename when alt is empty
explanation: Empty `alt=''` is a valid technique to mark an image as decorative; screen readers skip it, which is correct if the image is purely visual and not informative.

question: A responsive image uses ``. Which is downloaded on a 768px viewport?
options: small.jpg because the viewport is between 480w and 1024w
large.jpg because the image is 100vw
the browser selects based on device pixel ratio and connection speed
both small and large are downloaded and the browser chooses
explanation: The `sizes='100vw'` attribute tells the browser the image will be 100% of viewport width; on a 768px viewport, the browser selects the smallest source that is at least 768w, which is large.jpg.

question: Why might `` fail on older browsers?
options: webp format is not supported in older browsers and the image will not load
older browsers require a fallback image using picture element
webp requires a specific doctype or mime type
webp images need javascript to display
explanation: WebP is a modern image format; browsers that don't support it will fail to load the image, so fallbacks via `<picture>` element or server-side negotiation are necessary.

question: A `` element has `` followed by ``. On a dark-mode device, which image loads?
options: light.jpg because img is the fallback and always loads
dark.jpg because the media query matches
both images load and javascript chooses which to display
the media query is evaluated and only dark.jpg loads
explanation: The `<picture>` element selects the best `<source>` based on media queries and srcset; only the selected source (dark.jpg in this case) is downloaded.

question: An image has ``. What is a risk of lazy loading?
options: lazy loaded images are not indexed by search engines
the image may not load if javascript is disabled
lazy loading reduces initial page load but images appear late on scroll
images are cached differently, reducing browser storage
explanation: Lazy-loaded images are fetched only when needed, improving initial load time but potentially delaying image appearance when users scroll to them.

question: Why might an image with `` not be styled by page CSS?
options: svg images loaded via img tag are in their own document context and css does not cross-apply
svg requires a special namespace to accept css
img element cannot load svg files
svg css requires style tags inside the svg file
explanation: SVGs loaded via `` tag run in a restricted mode; external page CSS does not apply to them, so styling must be done inside the SVG file or via inline styles.

question: An image uses ``. A responsive site changes width to 50% via CSS. Why might the image aspect ratio distort?
options: html height and width attributes lock the aspect ratio, overriding css
css width changes the aspect ratio even if height is specified
the browser maintains the original aspect ratio if both dimensions are set
aspect ratio distortion is prevented when both html attributes are set
explanation: HTML attributes set the intrinsic aspect ratio, but CSS dimensions override rendering size independently; if CSS changes width without proportional height, distortion occurs.

question: An image uses ``. Why is duplicate alt and title redundant?
options: alt and title serve the same purpose and only alt is needed
title is shown on hover and alt on missing images
alt is for accessibility, title is for user hover tooltips; both are useful but not necessary duplicates
having both creates performance overhead
explanation: While `alt` is for accessibility and `title` for hover tooltips, duplicating the same text is redundant; `title` should provide additional context not in `alt`.

question: Why might `` improve page performance?
options: async decoding allows other content to render while the image is decoded
images are decoded on a separate thread faster than normal decoding
async decoding prevents layout shift from image loading
browser prioritizes other resources while async decoding proceeds
explanation: The `decoding='async'` attribute hints to the browser that image decoding can happen asynchronously, allowing page rendering to continue without waiting for the image to decode.

question: A map image uses `` with ``. What does the area element do?
options: it defines a clickable region within the image that links to a url
it creates an overlay on the image
it requires javascript to function
map and area are deprecated and canvas should be used instead
explanation: The `<map>` and `<area>` elements define clickable regions (hotspots) on an image, allowing different parts to link to different URLs.

question: A link has `<a href='https://example.com' target='_blank' rel='noopener'>`. Which security vulnerability does rel='noopener' prevent?
options: prevents the new window from accessing window.opener and navigating the original page
prevents the new page from reading cookies from the original domain
prevents cross-origin requests from the new window
prevents the new window from closing the original tab
explanation: Without `rel='noopener'`, the new window retains a reference to `window.opener`, allowing the new page to navigate or manipulate the original window, creating a security risk.

question: A site uses `Download` to link to an image. When clicked, what happens?
options: the image is downloaded to the user's device
the image is displayed in a new page or tab
the browser navigates to the image url like any link
behavior depends on whether the server sends content-disposition header
explanation: An anchor tag navigates to the URL; whether the image is displayed or downloaded depends on the server's Content-Disposition header and the browser's file-handling rules.

question: A link uses `<a href='page.php?id=5&name=test'>`. Why might a database lookup fail?
options: url parameters must be separated by semicolons, not ampersands
php does not parse query strings in href attributes
the ampersand should be escaped as & in html
the php file cannot receive multiple parameters in url
explanation: In HTML, `&` must be escaped as `&` to be valid markup; some parsers may misinterpret unescaped `&` as the start of an entity reference.

question: A page uses `<link rel='canonical' href='https://example.com/page'>` pointing to itself. Why is this redundant?
options: canonical should point to a different version of the page, not itself
canonical links are ignored by search engines when pointing to the same url
search engines already treat the current page as canonical
having any canonical tag makes pointing to self unnecessary
explanation: The canonical link is for indicating the preferred version when duplicate content exists; self-referencing is redundant since the page is inherently canonical.

question:
Why might `Back to Top` not work if the page has no `` or `

options: the anchor fragment is ignored if no matching id or name exists
modern browsers create an implicit top anchor
hash navigation only works for ids, not name attributes
the link will cause a JavaScript error
explanation: Fragment identifiers require a matching element with an `id` attribute or (in older HTML) a `name` attribute; if neither exists, the link is ineffective.

question: A link uses `<a href='http://example.com' download>`. Which file is downloaded?
options: the entire webpage is downloaded as an html file
the resource pointed to by the href is downloaded with its name
the browser prompts for a filename and downloads the resource
download attribute requires a filename, this link is invalid
explanation: The `download` attribute (with or without a value) causes the browser to download the linked resource instead of navigating to it, using the provided name or the resource name.

question: A page has `<link rel='prefetch' href='next-page.html'>`. Why might this not prefetch on slow networks?
options: prefetch requires a minimum bandwidth threshold before fetching
prefetch is a hint, not a guarantee; browsers may ignore it based on connection speed or user settings
prefetch only works for css and js, not html
slow networks require rel='preload' instead
explanation: The `prefetch` directive is a performance hint; browsers may choose not to prefetch on slow connections, low-battery devices, or when data-saving mode is enabled.

question: Why should `<a href='data:text/html,<script>alert(1)</script>' target='_blank'>` be avoided?
options: data: urls are blocked by default in all browsers
data urls with script content execute in the context of the current origin
target=_blank is incompatible with data: urls
data urls are deprecated and will be removed
explanation: Data URLs with HTML/script content execute in the same origin context, potentially creating XSS vulnerabilities if user input is embedded.

question: A site uses `<a href='//cdn.example.com/file.js'>` instead of `https://cdn.example.com/file.js`. What advantage does this provide?
options: protocol-relative urls use http if the page is http, https if the page is https
protocol-relative urls load faster because they skip protocol negotiation
protocol-relative urls bypass the browser cache
there is no advantage; protocol-relative urls are obsolete
explanation: Protocol-relative URLs (starting with `//`) automatically use the same protocol as the current page, allowing http/https compatibility without explicitly specifying the protocol.

question: A navigation link is marked as `<a href='/about' aria-current='page'>`. Which screen reader behavior changes?
options: the link is not announced as clickable; screen readers read it as static text
screen readers announce the link with an indication that it is the current page
the link is visually highlighted to match current page
aria-current only works with role='navigation' parent
explanation: The `aria-current='page'` attribute signals to assistive tech that this link represents the currently viewed page, allowing users to know their location in navigation.

question:
A page uses microdata with `
John
`. Why does search engine not parse it correctly?
options: search engines do not support microdata and require json-ld
the itemtype url must match the property names exactly
the itemprop value must be a valid url, not plain text
search engines parse this correctly; the structure is valid
explanation: The microdata structure is valid; search engines like Google parse microdata with itemscope/itemtype/itemprop correctly to extract structured data.

question: A recipe uses JSON-LD: `<script type='application/ld+json'>{"@context":"https://schema.org", "@type":"Recipe"}</script>`. Which format is this?
options: microdata markup
json-ld is a json-based structured data format
rdfa format
hcalendar format
explanation: JSON-LD (JSON for Linking Data) is a JSON-based format for structured data; it is embedded in `<script>` tags and is machine-parseable by search engines and crawlers.

question:
A page uses `
Jane Doe
`. What microformat is this?
options: hcalendar
hcard is a microformat for contact information
microdata format
open graph markup
explanation: hCard is a microformat using HTML classes (vcard, fn, etc.) to mark up contact details like names, addresses, and phone numbers in a machine-readable way.

question: A page uses `<meta property='og:image' content='image.jpg'>`. What does this enable?
options: search engines use it for image indexing
social media platforms display a preview image when the page is shared
schema.org parsers extract image metadata
the og property is deprecated and ignored
explanation: Open Graph (og:) meta tags control how social platforms (Facebook, Twitter, etc.) display previews when a link is shared, including title, image, and description.

question: A page uses `<link rel='schema.org' href='https://schema.org/Article'>`. Why is this redundant?
options: schema.org is always available and the link is unnecessary
the schema namespace should be declared via itemtype, not a link
search engines know schema.org without explicit link declaration
all three reasons above are correct
explanation: Schema.org is a standard namespace that search engines recognize without explicit declaration; linking to the schema.org URL is redundant when using itemtype or @context.

question:
A breadcrumb uses `
Home
`. Why might this fail validation?
options: breadcrumblist requires position properties on each item
itemlistelements must be wrapped in separate itemscope divs
the structure is valid and should validate correctly
schema.org types must be in lowercase
explanation: Schema.org BreadcrumbList requires each item to have position and url properties; a flat list of items without individual itemscope and properties is incomplete.

question: A page uses `<meta name='twitter:card' content='summary_large_image'>`. What does this control?
options: how the page appears when shared on twitter
twitter crawlers index the page differently
the page is optimized for twitter's search algorithm
twitter:card is not a real meta tag
explanation: Twitter Card meta tags control how links appear when shared on Twitter, including card type (summary, image, player), title, description, and image preview.

question:
A page uses RDFa: `
Title
`. Why is RDFa less common than JSON-LD?
options: rdfa is harder to write and maintain in html
search engines do not support rdfa
json-ld is easier to implement and separate from html markup
rdfa is deprecated
explanation: JSON-LD is easier to embed without polluting HTML markup, making it the preferred format for structured data; RDFa requires namespaces and attributes scattered through the DOM.

question: A product page uses `<meta property='og:price:amount' content='19.99'>`. Which social platforms use this metadata?
options: all social platforms support product pricing metadata
only facebook and pinterest use commerce-related og tags
og:price is not a standard open graph property
search engines use it for shopping results, not social platforms
explanation: Open Graph does not define og:price as a standard property; e-commerce metadata is better handled via schema.org markup (Product type) or platform-specific meta tags.

question: A page embeds `<script type='application/ld+json'>` twice with different @type values. How does the search engine interpret this?
options: only the first json-ld block is parsed
both blocks are merged and parsed as a single entity
each block is parsed separately as distinct entities
duplicate json-ld blocks cause a parsing error
explanation: Multiple JSON-LD blocks are parsed independently; each can describe different entities or add complementary data, allowing rich markup for multiple types on one page.

question: A page has `<header><nav></nav></header>` followed by `<nav></nav>` in the footer. Why might a screen reader user be confused?
options: nav elements cannot repeat on the same page
the outline algorithm sees both as top-level navigations with no hierarchy
header should not contain nav, header is only for introductory content
multiple nav elements require unique aria-label to distinguish them
explanation: Multiple `<nav>` elements should each have a descriptive `aria-label` (e.g., 'Main navigation', 'Footer navigation') so assistive tech can differentiate them in landmarks.

question: A blog post is structured as `<article><section>...</section></article>` instead of nested `<article><article>...</article></article>`. Which is semantically correct for comments?
options: section is correct for comments because they are not independent content
article is correct for each comment because each is self-contained content
both are wrong, comments should use div with aria-labelledby
the choice does not affect semantics, only css styling
explanation: Each comment is independently distributable and reusable content, so `<article>` is semantically correct; `<section>` groups related content but implies a heading.

question: Why should `<aside>` not be used to wrap a related-products sidebar in a shopping cart checkout?
options: aside is only for pull quotes, not advertisements
checkout product suggestions are tangentially related, not off-topic
aside implies content that is supplementary but the products are primary to purchase flow
aside requires a heading to clarify its purpose
explanation: In checkout context, suggested products are part of the main transaction flow, not tangential; `<aside>` is reserved for content that could be removed without breaking understanding of the main content.

question: A document has `<main>` wrapping both article content and a newsletter signup form. A screen reader user jumps to main content. What happens?
options: the browser only exposes the article to the main landmark, form is hidden
both article and form are included in the main landmark
only one main element is allowed per document so the form is ignored
screen reader assistive technology skips form elements inside main
explanation: The `<main>` element contains both the article and form, so a screen reader jumping to main content will announce the entire region including both.

question: A developer uses `<div class='header'>` instead of `<header>`. Why would an accessible name tree differ?
options: div has no implicit role, so it is transparent to accessibility tree; header has implicit role banner
screen readers announce header with audio cue, div requires explicit announcement
header creates a region landmark, div does not
div and header are synonymous for assistive tech, only presentation differs
explanation: A `<div>` with a class is semantically neutral to assistive tech; `<header>` has the implicit role `banner`, making it navigable as a landmark and improving document outline.

question:
Which element correctly wraps `

Featured Products

` and a list of items without being a sectioning context?
options: div
section
article
main
explanation: A `<div>` is neutral and does not create a sectioning context; `<section>` / `<article>` / `<main>` all create sectioning contexts that affect heading hierarchy in the outline algorithm.

question: A page uses `<nav>` for a breadcrumb trail at the top and `<nav>` for the main menu. A keyboard user presses a skip link. What should happen?
options: skip link jumps to main content, bypassing both nav elements

explanation: Both min-width and max-width conditions must be true; matches viewports 600px <= width <= 900px.

options: Ignored on retina displays
Matches high-DPI devices
Applies to all screen sizes
Requires viewport meta tag
explanation: min-device-pixel-ratio: 2 targets high-DPI displays (retina, 2x, 3x); useful for serving high-resolution images.

question:
Why is the viewport meta tag critical for media queries?
```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```
options: Media queries ignore it
Sets viewport width to device width for proper breakpoints
Only needed on mobile
Deprecated in modern browsers
explanation: Without this meta tag, mobile browsers default to a wide viewport (often 980px), making min-width breakpoints match incorrectly.

options: Only on dark wallpapers
When OS or browser prefers dark mode
Always on mobile
Browser must have dark-mode toggle
explanation: prefers-color-scheme respects the operating system's dark/light preference; users set this in OS settings or browser.

options: First (comma)
Second (or keyword)
Third (pipe)
All are valid
explanation: Comma (,) is the OR operator in media queries; each comma-separated condition is evaluated separately.

options: Both are identical
device-width is always larger
width respects zoom, device-width doesn't
device-width is deprecated
explanation: width is the actual viewport width (affected by zoom); device-width is the physical screen size (ignored zoom).

options: 768px exactly
768px and above
768px and below
Any viewport (matches all)
explanation: The width property without min/max is an exact match; only viewports precisely 768px wide match.

options: Feature queries check CSS support
Media queries check CSS support
Both do the same thing
Feature queries are deprecated
explanation: @supports checks browser CSS feature support; media queries check device/viewport characteristics; use both for robust layouts.

options: Exact numbers depend on design
Tablet usually 600-900px range
Desktop starts 1024px+
All sizes work equally
explanation: Breakpoints should align with design intent, not device names; common patterns are 640px (tablet), 1024px (desktop), but always test and adjust.

options: No performance effect
Hints to browser to create rendering layer
Apply to every animated element
Only for GPU acceleration
explanation: will-change tells browsers to prepare for changes; use sparingly (3-4 elements max) to optimize animation performance.

options: No difference in performance
transform uses GPU, left causes reflow
left is always faster
Depends on element size
explanation: transform and opacity bypass reflow/repaint (composite-only); left/top trigger layout recalculation on every frame.

options: No performance issue
Read (offsetWidth) forces layout, write forces reflow; repeating thrashes
Only affects old browsers
Browser optimizes automatically
explanation: Reading layout then writing forces sync reflow 100 times; batching all reads then all writes prevents thrashing.

options: No effect
Isolates element; prevents reflow affecting outside
Only layout containment matters
Requires vendor prefixes
explanation: contain: layout style paint tells browser element won't affect siblings; enables independent reflow and repaint optimization.

options: No performance benefit
Prevents invisible text delay; shows fallback immediately
Always slower than sync
Requires font preload
explanation: font-display: swap shows fallback while font loads, avoiding invisible text (FOIT); improves perceived performance.

question:
How does splitting CSS into multiple files impact performance?
```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="main.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="theme.css">
```
options: More files = faster
More HTTP requests; use sparingly or bundle
Browser parallelizes; always better
No difference with HTTP/2
explanation: More CSS files = more requests (overhead); modern builds bundle CSS; HTTP/2 helps but single file still optimal.

question:
What is the purpose of critical CSS, and when is it extracted?
```html
<style>/* Critical above-fold CSS inlined */</style>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="rest.css">
```
options: No purpose
Inline above-fold CSS to unblock rendering
Extract unused CSS
Only needed on slow connections
explanation: Critical CSS (above-fold styles) is inlined in HTML head; non-critical deferred, reducing First Contentful Paint.

question:
How do render-blocking stylesheets affect page load, and how is this mitigated?
```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> <!-- blocks rendering -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="print.css" media="print"> <!-- doesn't block -->
```
options: Stylesheets never block
Parser pauses rendering until CSS loaded
Can defer non-critical CSS via media queries
Both 2 and 3
explanation: CSS blocks rendering by default; media queries, async loading, or preload hints mitigate blocking.

question:
Why should selector specificity be kept low for performance?
```css
.page .section .article .paragraph .text { } /* high specificity, deep match */
.text { } /* low specificity, fast match */
```
options: No performance difference
Simple selectors match faster
Specificity affects runtime, not match time
Deep selectors always slower
explanation: Selector complexity has minimal impact on modern browsers; cascade and reflows matter more than selector depth.

options: Minification removes whitespace
Tree-shaking removes unused selectors
Manual deletion required
Both 1 and 2
explanation: Minification removes whitespace; tree-shaking (PurgeCSS, Tailwind) removes unused rules by analyzing HTML.

options: em and rem are identical
em is relative to parent, rem to root
rem is relative to parent, em to root
Both ignore root context
explanation: em scales relative to parent font-size (1.5em = 30px); rem always scales relative to root (html) font-size.

question:
Why might using viewport width units (vw) cause horizontal scroll on narrow screens?
```css
.box { width: 100vw; }
```
options: 100vw equals 100% width
100vw includes scrollbar width
vw is not supported
Always correct on mobile
explanation: 100vw includes the scrollbar width; on small screens, it's wider than the viewport, causing overflow and horizontal scroll.

options: Height auto maintains aspect ratio
Requires padding-bottom hack
aspect-ratio property handles it
Video element ignores CSS
explanation: The modern aspect-ratio CSS property (aspect-ratio: 16 / 9) maintains aspect ratio; legacy approach used padding-bottom hack.

options: max-width is ignored on small screens
max-width caps width at 1200px
Requires media queries to work
Overrides width property
explanation: max-width sets an upper limit; on large screens, width stays at max-width; on small screens, 90% applies (whichever is smaller).

question:
What does the clamp() function do for responsive typography?
```css
font-size: clamp(1rem, 2vw, 2rem);
```
options: Sets exact font size
Scales between 1rem and 2rem, preferring 2vw
Always uses minimum value
Requires fallback font-size
explanation: clamp(min, preferred, max) uses preferred value if it falls between min/max; otherwise uses min or max.

options: This approach always works
height: auto prevents reflow
Requires explicit aspect-ratio
Set max-width to prevent oversizing
explanation: width: 100% with height: auto can cause layout shift if height isn't known; aspect-ratio or explicit dimensions prevent shift.

options: Container queries check parent width
Media queries check viewport only
Components can adapt independently of viewport
All are equivalent
explanation: Container queries adapt based on container width, not viewport; same component renders differently in different containers.

options: 20px minimum
44-48px recommended
Depends on device
No standard size
explanation: WCAG 2.5.5 recommends 44x44 CSS pixels minimum for touch targets; 40px is slightly below but often acceptable.

options: Always use padding percentages
Legacy technique; use aspect-ratio now
Padding is unrelated to layout
Only for mobile
explanation: The padding-bottom percentage hack maintained aspect ratio before aspect-ratio property; modern approach is simpler and cleaner.

options: width: 50% overrides flex
flex: 1 distributes space, width is ignored
width: 50% sets minimum
Both properties conflict
explanation: In flex containers, flex property controls size distribution; width is treated as initial size hint or min-width depending on context.

question:
What is the specificity value of this selector?
```css
#main .box > p::first-line
```
explanation: Specificity is: 1 ID (#main) = 100, 1 class (.box) = 10, 1 pseudo-element (::first-line) = 1, 1 element (p) = 1; total = 0,1,2,1.

question:
What will this attribute selector match?
```css
input[type="text"]
```
options: All input elements
Inputs with type attribute
Inputs with type exactly matching 'text'
Inputs starting with 'text'
explanation: The attribute exact-match selector [attr="value"] requires the attribute value to match exactly; 'text' vs 'email' are different.

question:
When would :first-child fail to select an element while :first-of-type succeeds? ```html

Title

First paragraph

``` ```css p:first-child { color: blue; } p:first-of-type { color: red; } ```
options: Both would fail
first-child matches, first-of-type fails
first-child fails, first-of-type matches
Both match, red wins
explanation: p:first-child fails because the first child is h2, not p; p:first-of-type succeeds because p is the first p element among siblings.

options: First excludes .active, second excludes both
Same behavior in all browsers
Second uses legacy :not() syntax
Chaining selectors in :not() not supported
explanation: The :not() selector only accepts a single simple selector in older specs; modern browsers support :not(.active, .disabled) but older ones require chaining :not(.active):not(.disabled).

question:
In terms of CSS performance, which selector is typically most expensive to process?
```css
* { } /* universal */
div p span { } /* descendant chain */
.container .item { } /* class descendant */
#header nav { } /* id descendant */
```
options: Universal selector
Long descendant chains
Class selectors
ID selectors
explanation: The universal selector (*) targets every element in the DOM, forcing style recalculation on all nodes; browser optimizations matter more than selector type.

question:
What will be the computed text color of the span? ```html

Colored text

``` ```css p.text { color: blue; } #main .highlight { color: green; } span.highlight { color: red; } ```
options: blue (element + class)
green (ID specificity higher)
red (last rule wins)
conflict: specificity tie
explanation: Specificity: p.text = 0,0,1,1 (11); #main .highlight = 0,1,1,0 (110); span.highlight = 0,0,1,1 (11); ID rule wins with highest specificity.

options: ::before
::after
::selection
None, all can be styled
explanation: ::selection can only accept background-color, background, and color; text-specific properties like font or text-decoration are not applicable.

question:
When testing this, which element will match :nth-child(2)? ```html
  • Item 1
  • Item 2
  • Item 3
``` ```css li:nth-child(2) { color: red; } ```
options: Item 1 (first li)
Item 2 (second li, has class)
Item 3 (skips li.skip)
No match (class blocks selector)
explanation: nth-child counts all children by position regardless of class; the second child is the li with class='skip', so it matches and turns red.

options: Both do the same thing
+ matches first sibling, ~ matches all
+ matches next sibling, ~ matches all following
~ is invalid syntax
explanation: The adjacent sibling combinator (+) matches only the immediate next sibling; the general sibling combinator (~) matches all following siblings.

question: Given `#nav .item` (id + class) versus `.menu .item.active` (two classes), which selector has higher specificity?
options: #nav .item, because an id outweighs multiple classes
the one with more classes always wins
they are equal in specificity
whichever appears later in the file
explanation: Specificity compares id count first, and one id beats any number of classes.

question: You have a feature branch that was created from main three weeks ago. You want to update it with the latest changes from main, but you need to preserve the feature branch's commit sequence without interleaving main commits. Which approach is correct?
options: Use git rebase main to replay feature commits on top of the updated main
Use git merge main --squash to combine all changes into a single commit
Use git pull origin main to fetch and merge in one step
Use git fetch origin && git reset --hard origin/main to match remote exactly
explanation: Rebase replays the feature branch's commits one by one on top of main's tip, creating a linear history; merge would create a merge commit interleaving the histories.

question: You accidentally committed changes to the production branch instead of a feature branch. The commit has not been pushed yet. You want to move the commit to a new branch and reset production to its previous state. What is the safest sequence?
options: Create a new branch from the current HEAD, then reset production to HEAD~1 using git reset --hard
Use git revert to undo the commit on production
Delete the production branch and recreate it from origin
Rebase production onto origin/production to remove the commit
explanation: Create a new branch at the commit to preserve it, then reset production; the commit is now safely on the feature branch and production is restored.

question: Your repository has a branch naming convention: feature/*, bugfix/*, and hotfix/*. You want to prevent developers from pushing directly to main and require a pull request. Which Git configuration or server-side mechanism enforces this?
options: Configure branch protection rules on GitHub/GitLab to require pull request reviews and block direct pushes to main
Set core.protectBranches to true in .gitconfig
Create a pre-push hook that blocks commits to main
Configure push.default to upstream to enforce upstream tracking
explanation: Branch protection is a server-side feature provided by GitHub, GitLab, or similar platforms; it prevents pushes regardless of local configuration.

question: You have a branch that was based on main, but you realize it should have been based on a different branch (develop). The branch has ten commits. How do you rebase it onto develop without losing work?
options: Use git rebase --onto develop main to replay commits from main..HEAD onto develop
Delete the branch and recreate it from develop
Use git merge develop to merge develop into the feature branch
Manually cherry-pick each commit onto develop
explanation: rebase --onto <newbase> <oldbase> replays commits from oldbase..HEAD onto newbase; this correctly transfers all ten commits to the new base.

question: You want to delete a local branch, but Git refuses with the error 'branch not fully merged into HEAD'. Your feature is complete and you are sure you want to delete it. What is the safest verification before using force-delete?
options: Run git log main..branch-name to check if there are any unique commits; if empty, it is safe to force-delete with -D
Use git branch -d to confirm the deletion
Check the branch's remote tracking status with git branch -vv
Run git merge --ff-only to ensure the branch is fully merged
explanation: git log main..branch-name shows commits unique to the branch; if empty, all work is already in main and force-delete (-D) is safe.

question: You have a feature branch with many small commits (work-in-progress). Before merging to main, you want to clean up the history into logical commits. Which operation accomplishes this without losing any work?
options: Use git rebase -i to interactively squash, reorder, and edit commits before merge
Use git merge --squash to combine everything into one commit
Use git reset --soft HEAD~N to stage all changes and commit once
Cherry-pick individual commits onto a new branch
explanation: Interactive rebase (-i) allows fine-grained control over commits (squash, reorder, reword); merge --squash loses the commit sequence and must be redone after merge.

question: You push a feature branch to remote and a colleague starts working on it. Later, you realize the commits have mistakes and you want to force-push the corrected history. What must you communicate to your colleague to avoid losing their work?
options: Tell them to save their work locally, then pull and merge the corrected history after the force-push
Force-push immediately; Git will detect and reject conflicting work automatically
Ask them to delete their local copy and re-clone
Revert commits instead of rewriting history to preserve their branch state
explanation: Force-push rewrites remote history; collaborators must save local work, reset to the new remote, and re-apply their changes or merge them in.

question: Your repository has both main and develop branches. A feature branch created from develop needs a critical fix from main. You want to avoid merging all of main into develop. What approach is most precise?
options: Use git cherry-pick to apply the specific critical commit(s) from main onto develop and the feature branch
Merge all of main into develop
Rebase develop onto main
Create a new branch from main for the feature
explanation: cherry-pick selects individual commits; this avoids pulling in unrelated changes and keeps the develop branch's intended scope.

question: You track a remote branch with git branch --set-upstream, but the remote branch is deleted. Your local branch becomes stale. How do you update your local tracking references to reflect the deleted remote branch?
options: Run git fetch --prune to remove stale remote tracking branches
Manually delete the remote tracking branch with git branch -dr origin/branch-name
Run git branch --unset-upstream to remove the tracking reference
Pull from the remote to refresh the tracking references
explanation: git fetch --prune automatically deletes local remote-tracking branches (refs/remotes/origin/*) if they no longer exist on the remote.

question: You have a branch with a detached HEAD after rebasing. You want to reconnect the detached HEAD to a branch reference. What is the correct command?
options: Use git branch branch-name or git checkout -b branch-name to create a branch reference at the current HEAD
Use git merge to combine the detached HEAD with an existing branch
Run git attach-head to reattach the detached HEAD
Use git reset --hard to reset to the branch state
explanation: git branch branch-name creates a new branch reference pointing to the current detached HEAD; git checkout -b does the same and switches to it immediately.

question: A pull request introduces a performance regression. As a reviewer, you notice the issue in the code before it reaches production. How should you document this finding in the review to make it actionable?
options: Comment with a specific example (code snippet or benchmark), suggest a concrete fix, and mark it as a 'blocking issue' or 'changes requested' to prevent merge
Say 'I think this might be slow' without details
Approve anyway and file a separate issue to fix later
Reject the entire PR without explanation
explanation: Specific, actionable comments with examples guide the developer to fix the issue immediately; marking as blocking ensures it is resolved before merge.

question: During code review, you spot a subtle bug that the author likely introduced by accident. Before rejecting the PR, what is the best way to help them learn from the mistake?
options: Explain why the bug occurs, provide a corrected example, and suggest testing strategies to catch similar issues in the future
Just say 'bug' and mark it blocking
Fix the bug in a follow-up commit yourself
Tell them to find the bug on their own
explanation: Educational feedback fosters learning and trust; explaining root causes helps prevent similar issues in future code.

question: A colleague asks you to review their PR, and you notice it mixes refactoring changes with feature changes. The code is correct, but the mix makes the PR hard to review. How should you handle this?
options: Request they split the PR into separate ones (refactoring + feature) so each can be reviewed independently and reverted if needed
Approve both changes together
Reject the PR entirely
Approve if the code works
explanation: Separating concerns makes reviews and debugging easier; refactoring PRs can be fast-tracked and feature PRs receive focused review.

question: You are reviewing a PR and notice the code follows a pattern that differs from the team's established conventions. The code is technically correct but inconsistent. Should you request changes?
options: Yes, if the inconsistency impacts readability or maintainability; mention the convention and suggest aligning; document it in the team's style guide if missing
No, always approve correct code regardless of style
Reject the PR for style alone
Fix it yourself without feedback
explanation: Consistency reduces cognitive load for future maintainers; reviewing for conventions enforces team standards while helping the author improve.

question: During review, you find a complex algorithm that is correct but difficult to understand. The author is confident it is optimal. How should you approach this as a reviewer?
options: Request clarification with a comment asking them to add documentation or a simplified explanation; if still unclear after they clarify, suggest a more readable approach
Trust their judgment and approve
Require them to rewrite it immediately
Approve with a mental note to refactor later
explanation: Asking for explanation serves dual purposes: you verify understanding and they document complexity for future maintainers.

question: A pull request adds a new dependency to the project. As a reviewer, what concerns should you evaluate before approving?
options: Evaluate necessity (does it solve a real problem), maintenance status (is it actively maintained), licensing (compatible with project), size/performance impact, and security (known vulnerabilities)
Approve if it works
Count the number of lines it adds
Check if it is popular on GitHub
explanation: New dependencies introduce technical debt, attack surface, and maintenance burden; thorough evaluation prevents downstream issues.

question: You are reviewing a PR and notice the author has not added tests for the new functionality. They claim the code 'is tested manually.' How should you respond?
options: Request automated tests (unit, integration, or end-to-end) before approval; manual testing does not scale and misses regressions
Approve if manual testing passed
Write the tests yourself
Request test plan documentation instead of code
explanation: Automated tests provide scalable verification, prevent regressions, and serve as documentation; manual testing alone is insufficient for production code.

question: You approve a pull request with a comment suggesting an optional improvement. The author implements it immediately and pushes a new commit. Should they expect you to re-review?
options: Yes, you should re-review the new change to verify the implementation matches your suggestion and did not introduce issues
No, your approval is final and covers all future commits
They should request approval from someone else
Re-review is never necessary
explanation: Optional suggestions still require verification when implemented; re-review ensures the implementation is correct and complete.

question: A pull request contains changes you are not qualified to review (e.g., complex ML algorithm, infrastructure code). How should you handle this as an assigned reviewer?
options: Acknowledge the request, request a specialist reviewer, and step back; verify that the PR received expert review before approving
Approve without understanding
Reject because you cannot review
Ignore the PR
explanation: Assigning specialist reviewers ensures domain expertise; this is a sign of a healthy review culture, not a failure.

question: You review a PR and approve it, but later discover a critical bug in the approved code. What are your responsibilities?
options: Report the issue immediately, take responsibility for the review miss, help create a fix, and discuss how to improve review practices to catch similar issues
Blame the author for writing buggy code
Hide the bug and hope no one notices
Ask the author to take full responsibility
explanation: Code review is a shared responsibility; ownership of the miss strengthens team trust and leads to process improvements.

question: You run git log and see a commit that breaks the build, but git bisect repeatedly identifies an earlier commit as the culprit. The issue is intermittent and depends on file system state. What does this suggest about the commits?
options: The culprit commit introduced a non-deterministic bug that is masked by ordering or timing; the later commit may expose it, but the root cause is earlier
git bisect is faulty and cannot be trusted
The build system is broken and needs reconfiguration
The commits are corrupted and should be reset
explanation: Bisect finds the first commit where a test fails; if failures are non-deterministic (race conditions, file system state), the identified commit may expose a latent bug from earlier.

question: You want to find all commits that modified a specific file but were later reverted or deleted. Running git log on the file shows only current commits. How do you discover deleted commits?
options: Use git log --diff-filter=D to find deletion commits, or git log -S<string> to find commits that changed specific code
Run git reflog to view all branch movements
Use git log --all to include unreachable commits
Check the backup branch from before the deletion
explanation: git log --diff-filter=D finds commits that deleted files; git log -S searches for commits that introduced/removed specific code strings.

question: You want to extract all commits that touch a specific directory and apply them to another repository. Using git format-patch and git am, you generate patches, but one patch fails to apply. The failure is in the middle of the series. What is your strategy?
options: Use git am --continue after fixing the conflict, or use git am --abort to skip the problematic patch and resume
Regenerate all patches and start over
Manually merge the problematic commit
Use git apply with force flag to bypass conflict checks
explanation: git am --continue resumes after you resolve conflicts in the working directory; git am --abort cancels the current patch and skips to the next.

question: You use git reflog to see that HEAD was at commit X three commits ago, but that commit is not in git log. What does this indicate about commit X?
options: Commit X is not reachable from the current branch (orphaned or on a deleted branch), but still exists in the object database and can be recovered
Commit X was corrupted and deleted
Commit X is on a different remote branch
Commit X never existed and reflog is showing a false entry
explanation: Reflog shows all HEAD movements regardless of reachability; unreachable commits persist until garbage collection and can be recovered via reflog.

question: You need to find the first commit that introduced a bug in a specific function. Running git log -S to search for the function name returns hundreds of commits across many branches. How do you narrow the search to just the commits where the function was added (not modified)?
options: Use git log -S<function> --diff-filter=A to find only the commit that Added the function
Run git log --all to search all branches
Use git log -p to view full diffs of each commit
Filter manually by reviewing each commit's changes
explanation: --diff-filter=A returns only commits that added files or hunks; combined with -S, this finds the exact commit where code was introduced.

question: You run git log --oneline and notice that a commit message is truncated to one line, but the commit has a multi-line message with a long body. You want to view the full message without seeing the diff. Which command shows the full commit message?
options: Use git log --format=fuller or git show <commit> to display the complete message with headers
Use git log -p to include the patch
Increase the terminal width to show more text
Use git log --all to load more message content
explanation: git log --format=fuller displays full author/commit metadata and full messages; git show commits full details without diff (unless -p is added).

question: Your repository has a very long history (100k commits) and git log runs slowly. You want to speed it up while still viewing recent commits. Which optimization should you apply?
options: Use git log --oneline -n 100 to limit results, or git log --simplify-by-decoration to show only tagged commits
Run git gc --aggressive to repack objects
Delete old commits using git filter-branch
Clone the repository with --depth to create a shallow copy
explanation: Limiting output (-n) or filtering (--simplify-by-decoration) reduces work without modifying history; gc optimizes storage but doesn't speed up this query.

question: You want to see all commits across all branches and tags, including unreachable commits from the past three days. Which git log options or reflog strategy gives you this view?
options: Use git log --all --reflog --since='3 days ago' to show all reachable commits plus recent reflog entries
Use git log --oneline to see the current branch
Run git fsck --lost-found to find dangling objects
Use git remote -v to list all remote commits
explanation: --all includes all branches and tags; --reflog adds recent HEAD movements; --since filters by timestamp to focus on the three-day window.

question: You use git blame to find who made a change, and it shows a commit from a different developer than expected. The change was supposed to come from a rebase or merge. How do you determine if this is a rebase/merge artifact or an actual change by that developer?
options: Use git log -p <commit> to review the full commit message and context; check if the commit message indicates a rebase or merge operation
Ask the developer directly
Use git show to view the commit's author
Run git log --oneline to see the commit sequence
explanation: Rebase and merge operations create new commits with the current author; reviewing the commit message and surrounding context reveals whether the change was rebased/merged.

question: After running git rebase -i to squash multiple commits, you realize you made a mistake in the interactive editor and exited without saving. The rebase is in progress but not yet applied. What is your recovery option?
options: Use git rebase --abort to cancel the rebase and restore the branch to its pre-rebase state
Run git rebase --continue to force the rebase to complete
Use git reset --hard to discard changes
Delete and recreate the branch
explanation: git rebase --abort cancels the operation and restores the branch; the original commits remain intact and nothing is lost.

question: You suspect a commit corrupted the repository's Git objects. The repository is still accessible but you want to verify object integrity. Which command checks for corruption?
options: Use git fsck --full to verify all Git objects and their references, reporting any missing or corrupted objects
Run git status to check the repository health
Use git verify-pack to check a specific pack file
Clone the repository to verify it
explanation: git fsck scans the entire object database and index; --full checks unreachable objects; it reports dangling or corrupt objects.
