explanation: Process curr immediately, then push children; left is pushed last (popped first), achieving pre-order: process node before children.

question: A stack is implemented using a dynamic array that doubles in capacity when full. Pushing n elements requires a total of how many array assignments in the amortized sense?
options: n assignments
2 times n assignments
log n assignments
n squared assignments
explanation: Amortized analysis: resizing happens at sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., doubling; total assignments = 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n ≈ 2n, which amortizes to O(n) or O(1) per push.

question: Implementing a stack using a linked list where push/pop operations interact with the head node. What is the space complexity of this stack for n elements?
options: constant space
linear space
logarithmic space
quadratic space
explanation: Each of the n elements requires a node with data and a next pointer; storing n elements always requires O(n) linear space.

question: Evaluating a postfix expression like '3 4 + 5 *' using a stack: when you encounter an operator, what must be true about stack size?
options: stack must have exactly one element
stack must have at least two elements
stack must be empty
stack size does not matter
explanation: Operators pop two operands from the stack; for valid postfix, when an operator is encountered, at least two elements must have been pushed.

question: A stack-based depth-first search (DFS) traversal of a tree with n nodes visits each node once. What is the time complexity?
options: logarithmic time
linear time
linearithmic time
quadratic time
explanation: DFS visits each of the n nodes exactly once and processes each edge once, giving O(n + edges) which is O(n) for trees.

question: Matching brackets in an expression like '(([]{}))' using a stack requires pushing opening brackets and popping for closing brackets. If the expression is invalid, what indicates the error?
options: stack is non-empty at the end
stack underflows or closing bracket type mismatch
stack overflows
no error can be detected
explanation: Stack underflow occurs when popping from an empty stack; bracket type mismatch occurs when opening and closing types differ; both signal invalid expressions.

question: Naive string matching checks if pattern P exists in text T by comparing at each position. What is time complexity?
options: O(n)
O(m)
O(n + m)
explanation: Tries n-m+1 positions; each check is O(m) comparisons; total is O((n-m+1) * m).

question: KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) algorithm uses an LPS (Longest Proper Prefix which is also Suffix) array. What does LPS accomplish?
options: Stores character frequencies
Skips redundant comparisons on mismatch
Pre-processes pattern for O(1) lookup
Detects cycles in pattern
explanation: LPS tells how many positions to advance without re-comparing; achieves O(n + m) by avoiding redundant work on mismatch.

question: Code: function includes(text, pattern) { for(let i=0; i<=text.length-pattern.length; i++) if(text.substr(i, pattern.length) === pattern) return true; return false; } What is the issue?
options: No issue; O(n+m)
substr creates new string, O(n*m) time
Missing edge case for empty pattern
Doesn't handle special characters
explanation: substr creates a copy (O(m)); repeated n times gives O(n*m); use char-by-char comparison for better performance.

question: Rabin-Karp algorithm uses rolling hash to match patterns. What is advantage over naive matching?
options: Always faster
Hash comparison is O(1) vs O(m) string comparison
Detects multiple patterns
Works only on numeric strings
explanation: Hash of pattern matches hash of text substring in O(1); reduces comparison to hash check, achieving O(n + m) average case.

question: Building LPS array for pattern 'ABAB' requires which values?
explanation: LPS[i] = length of longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also suffix: A(0), AB(0), ABA(1), ABAB(2).

question: Finding all occurrences of pattern in text requires collecting all match positions. Which algorithm is most efficient?
options: Naive O(n*m) but simplest
KMP O(n+m) for all matches
Boyer-Moore O(n) best case
Rabin-Karp with hashing
explanation: KMP maintains O(n+m) even for multiple matches by continuing after each find; ideal for all-occurrence queries.

question: Naive string matching checks a pattern P of length m against a text T of length n by trying all n-m+1 positions. Worst-case time complexity?
options: linear time
quadratic time in n and m
linearithmic time
cubic time
explanation: Each position requires O(m) character comparisons; n-m+1 positions means O(n*m) quadratic time in worst case.

question: Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm preprocesses a pattern to build a failure function (LPS array) allowing O(n+m) matching time. What does LPS represent?
options: longest previous substring
longest proper prefix which is also suffix
leftmost pattern shift
last possible start
explanation: LPS[i] stores the length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix, enabling intelligent skipping of failed matches.

question: Boyer-Moore algorithm for string matching skips characters using a bad-character rule (furthest right occurrence of a character in pattern). Why does this speed up matching?
options: it always checks backward
mismatches can skip multiple characters instead of one
Boyer-Moore is always linear time
it reduces pattern size
explanation: When a mismatch occurs, the bad-character rule skips based on the mismatched text character, potentially jumping multiple positions.

question: Rabin-Karp algorithm uses polynomial rolling hash to match patterns. A hash collision occurs when two different substrings hash to the same value. What is the risk?
options: no risk, hashing is perfect
false positives require confirming actual match
false negatives miss real matches
cannot be handled
explanation: Hash collisions are false positives; must verify the actual characters; real matches are never missed (no false negatives).

question: In-order traversal of binary search tree produces elements in which order?
options: Breadth-first level order
Ascending sorted order
Pre-order (parent before children)
Post-order (children before parent)
explanation: In-order traversal visits left subtree, then node, then right subtree; for BST this yields ascending sorted values.

question: Code: function inorder(node, result = []) { if(!node) return result; inorder(node.left, result); result.push(node.val); inorder(node.right, result); return result; } What traversal is this?
options: Pre-order
In-order
Post-order
Level-order
explanation: Process left, then push node, then right; this is exactly in-order traversal.

question: Pre-order traversal visits nodes in which sequence?
options: Left, node, right
Left, right, node
Node, left, right
Right, node, left
explanation: Pre-order processes the node first, then left subtree, then right subtree.

question: Level-order (breadth-first) traversal of binary tree requires which data structure for O(n) time?
options: Stack
Queue
Hash set
Linked list
explanation: Queue processes nodes level-by-level; FIFO order ensures each node is visited once in O(n).

question: Code: function postorder(node) { if(!node) return; postorder(node.left); postorder(node.right); console.log(node.val); } Tracing on tree [1, [2], [3]]: what is output order?
explanation: Post-order visits left, right, then node; for given tree: left subtree (2), right subtree (3), then root (1).

question: Morris in-order traversal is a space-efficient traversal achieving O(1) extra space. How does it avoid recursion stack?
options: Uses iterative array
Uses reverse pointers to parent
Uses temporary node pointers to create threading
Uses global variable for recursion
explanation: Morris traversal creates temporary pointers from rightmost node of left subtree back to current node, enabling traversal without stack.

question: Iterative pre-order traversal using a stack: push node, pop, process, then push right then left. Why push right before left?
options: To visit nodes in reverse
Stacks are LIFO so left is popped first, achieving correct order
Right should always be visited before left
Prevents infinite loops
explanation: Stack is LIFO; pushing right then left means left is popped first (on top), achieving left-before-right processing order.

question: Code: function levelorder(root) { if(!root) return []; const result = [], queue = [root]; while(queue.length) { const level = []; for(let i=0; i<queue.length; i++) { const node = queue.shift(); level.push(node.val); if(node.left) queue.push(node.left); if(node.right) queue.push(node.right); } result.push(level); } return result; } What is the issue?
options: No issue; correct level-order
shift() is O(n), making this O(n²)
Level processing is incorrect
Missing return statement
explanation: shift() requires O(n) reindexing per call; with n nodes, this becomes O(n²) instead of optimal O(n).

question: In-order traversal of a binary search tree visits nodes in sorted order. If recursive in-order traversal is called on a tree with n nodes, what is the time complexity?
options: logarithmic time
linear time
linearithmic time
quadratic time
explanation: Each of the n nodes is visited exactly once; at each node, a constant-time recursive call is made, yielding O(n) linear time.

question: Pre-order traversal can be used to copy a tree. Post-order traversal is better for deletion. Why is post-order used for deletion?
options: post-order is faster
post-order visits children before the parent
post-order is easier to understand
both are equally suitable
explanation: When deleting, you must free children before freeing the parent node; post-order ensures children are processed and freed first.

question: What is the time complexity of std::sort on a std::vector?
options: O(n)
O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst-case
O(n log n) guaranteed
depends on initial order
explanation: std::sort uses introsort (hybrid quicksort/heapsort); O(n log n) average but O(n^2) worst-case for pathological inputs.

question: What is the time complexity of std::binary_search on a sorted range?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
depends on the value searched
explanation: binary_search divides the range in half each step, achieving O(log n) time.

question: How does std::find perform compared to binary_search on an unsorted vector?
options: find is faster due to caching
find is O(n); binary_search requires sorted data
both are O(log n)
find is always slower
explanation: find performs linear search O(n) on unsorted data; binary_search requires pre-sorted data for O(log n).

question: What is the time complexity of constructing a std::set from an unsorted std::vector?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
depends on the vector size
explanation: Each insertion into the tree-based set is O(log n); n insertions result in O(n log n) total.

question: What does Big O notation describe?
options: the exact number of operations
the upper bound on growth rate of operations
the average-case performance only
memory usage only
explanation: Big O describes worst-case asymptotic complexity; O(n) means the algorithm grows proportionally with input size.

question: What is the space complexity of std::sort?
options: O(n)
O(log n) or O(n) depending on implementation
O(n log n)
explanation: std::sort uses introsort with O(log n) extra space for recursion stack; some implementations may use O(n).

question: What is the time complexity of inserting into the middle of a std::list?
options: O(1) after finding the position
O(n) to find the position
O(n) total always
O(log n)
explanation: Insertion itself is O(1), but finding the position in an unsorted list requires O(n) linear search.

question: Is std::stable_sort faster or slower than std::sort?
options: stable_sort is always faster
stable_sort is slower due to stability guarantee
same speed with different results
speed depends on data distribution
explanation: stable_sort maintains relative order of equal elements; this overhead makes it slower than unsorted sort.

question: What is the time complexity of std::remove from a vector?
options: O(n) to rearrange; does not actually erase
O(1) removal only
O(n^2) due to erase overhead
depends on the value
explanation: std::remove rearranges elements in-place O(n) but does not erase; erase-remove idiom calls erase after remove.

question: What is the amortized time complexity of push_back on a vector?
options: O(n) always
O(1) amortized due to exponential growth
O(log n)
O(n log n)
explanation: push_back is O(1) amortized; occasional O(n) reallocations are spread over many O(1) insertions.

question: Why is the RAII pattern considered fundamental to C++ resource management?
options: RAII uses global variables for cleanup
RAII ties resource lifetime to object scope, ensuring cleanup via destructors
RAII is only for file handles
RAII is deprecated in C++11
explanation: RAII couples resource acquisition (constructor) with release (destructor), guaranteeing cleanup even on exceptions.

question: What is the Rule of Three/Five/Zero?
options: three rules that must be followed always
either implement destructor/copy/move or none; if any, define all
zero classes should use inheritance
deprecated rule from C++98
explanation: If a class needs a custom destructor (to free resources), it must also define copy constructor/assignment and move semantics.

question: Why should you avoid naked pointers in modern C++?
options: pointers are slower than references
smart pointers clarify ownership and prevent leaks
pointers are not allowed in C++17
naked pointers are necessary for efficiency
explanation: Smart pointers make ownership explicit and automate cleanup, reducing bugs; prefer them to raw pointers.

question: What does PIMPL (Pointer to Implementation) achieve?
options: improves performance by inlining
hides implementation details behind a pointer, enabling binary compatibility
makes code more readable
prevents virtual function overhead
explanation: PIMPL separates interface from implementation, allowing internal changes without recompiling clients.

question: Why is const-correctness important?
options: it prevents all bugs
it documents intent and enables compiler-checked guarantees about immutability
const is only for documentation
const eliminates the need for testing
explanation: const specifies what a function/object must not modify; the compiler enforces this, catching unintended mutations.

question: What should you check for when performing integer division?
options: nothing; division by zero is handled automatically
whether the divisor is zero to avoid undefined behavior
whether the dividend is smaller than the divisor
integer division never fails
explanation: Division by zero is undefined behavior; check divisor is nonzero before dividing.

question: Why is returning objects by const reference sometimes problematic?
options: it is always safe
if the referenced object is local, it becomes a dangling reference
const prevents optimization
const references cannot be returned
explanation: Returning a const reference to a temporary or local variable creates a dangling reference.

question: What is the benefit of using enums over magic numbers?
options: enums are faster
enums provide type safety and readability
enums eliminate the need for variables
no real benefit
explanation: Enums create named constants with type safety, making code self-documenting and enabling compiler checks.

question: Why should error handling avoid returning error codes in favor of exceptions?
options: exceptions are always slower
exceptions ensure errors cannot be silently ignored
error codes are more efficient
C++ forbids error codes
explanation: Callers can ignore error codes; exceptions force handling (catch or propagate), preventing silent failures.

question: What is the purpose of static analysis tools like clang-tidy?
options: they improve runtime performance
they detect common bugs and style violations at compile time
they prevent undefined behavior completely
they are unnecessary for experienced programmers
explanation: Static analyzers catch mistakes before runtime, improving code quality and catching subtle issues humans miss.

question: What is the output of `for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) { if (i == 1) continue; cout << i; }`?
explanation: continue skips the rest of the loop iteration; i=0 prints 0, i=1 skips print, i=2 prints 2.

question: Does a `goto` statement inside a try block to outside the try block cause the destructor to run?
options: no; goto bypasses destructors
yes; destructors run during exception unwinding
yes; but only if compiler supports it
depends on whether goto targets a catch block
explanation: goto from try to outside triggers automatic cleanup of in-scope objects via their destructors.

question: In a do-while loop, when is the condition checked relative to body execution?
options: before first execution
after first execution
both before and after
never checked, only in for loops
explanation: do-while always executes the body at least once, then checks the condition to decide on repetition.

question: What happens if you use a variable declared in a switch case before entering that case?
options: undefined behavior
the variable is uninitialized
compilation error if no initialization crosses case boundary
C++17 allows it with structured bindings
explanation: Variables declared in a case without initialization cannot be skipped; the compiler forbids jumping over their declaration.

question: Can a switch statement have multiple default cases?
options: yes; all are tried in order
no; compilation error if more than one
yes; but only the first is used
only in C++17 and later
explanation: The default label is a target for the switch; having two results in a redefinition error at compile time.

question: Given `if (ptr) { /* A */ } else if (!ptr) { /* B */ }`, can both blocks execute?
options: yes, if ptr changes between checks
no; exactly one executes
both execute if ptr is null
undefined behavior
explanation: else-if forms a chain where at most one branch executes; the conditions are mutually exclusive.

question: What does a `switch` statement do if no case matches and there is no default?
options: exits the switch; no block executes
throws a runtime exception
executes the first case
undefined behavior
explanation: switch without a matching case and no default simply skips the entire statement.

question: Does the ternary operator `a ? b : c` short-circuit evaluation of b and c?
options: no; both are always evaluated
yes; only the chosen branch is evaluated
yes; but only if a is a compile-time constant
depends on compiler optimization
explanation: The ternary operator short-circuits: if a is true, c is not evaluated; if false, b is not evaluated.

question: In a range-based for loop `for (auto x : container)`, is the loop variable always a copy?
options: yes; auto always creates a copy
no; auto deduces by reference if declared auto&
yes; only auto& creates a reference
depends on whether container is const
explanation: auto x copies; auto& references; auto&& binds to temporaries; deduction follows template rules.

question: What does this print? `int i=0; switch(i){case 0: std::cout<<"a"; case 1: std::cout<<"b"; break; default: std::cout<<"c";}`
options: ab, because case 0 falls through to case 1
only a
abc
only c
explanation: Without a break after case 0, execution falls through into case 1 before the break, printing 'ab'.

question: Given `int x = INT_MAX; x += 1;`, what is the value of x and why?
options: undefined behavior with unpredictable result
wraps to INT_MIN due to two's complement overflow
throws an exception
remains INT_MAX
explanation: Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior in C++; the compiler can optimize or transform the code in unexpected ways.

question: What is the output of `sizeof(struct S { char a; int b; char c; })`? (assume 4-byte int, 1-byte char)
options: 6 bytes
9 bytes
12 bytes
8 bytes
explanation: Memory alignment padding is added: char(1) + 3 padding + int(4) + char(1) + 3 padding = 12 bytes total.

question: A `short` is guaranteed to be how many bits by the C++ standard?
options: exactly 16 bits
at least 16 bits
at least 8 bits
implementation-defined with no guarantee
explanation: The standard mandates sizeof(short) ≥ 2, meaning at least 16 bits, but exact width varies by platform.

question: What does `static_cast<int>(3.7)` produce and is it safe?
options: 4 via rounding, always safe
3 via truncation, safe but lossy
undefined, compiler-dependent
compilation error
explanation: Explicit casts truncate (discard fractional part); the conversion is well-defined but loses precision.

question: In `bool b = 5; int x = b;`, what is x and does conversion work both directions?
options: x is 1; bool accepts any integer via implicit narrowing
x is 1; bool narrows only 0 to false and nonzero to true
x is 5; implicit conversion preserves value
compilation error due to narrowing
explanation: Bool-to-int is safe (converts false→0, true→1); int-to-bool is also safe (0→false, nonzero→true).

question: What is the difference between `signed char` and `char` for negative values?
options: no difference; char is always signed
char signedness is implementation-defined; signed char is guaranteed signed
both are identical by standard
signed char cannot represent negative values
explanation: Plain `char` signedness depends on the compiler, but `signed char` and `unsigned char` are always deterministic.

question: Given `uint8_t a = 200, b = 100; uint8_t c = a + b;`, what is c?
options: undefined behavior
compilation error
explanation: Unsigned overflow wraps modulo 2^n; 300 mod 256 = 44, a well-defined value.

question: Can you safely reinterpret_cast a `double*` to `int*` and read the bits?
options: yes, always; both are numeric types
yes, but only on little-endian systems
no; violates strict aliasing and causes undefined behavior
only if compiler flag disables strict aliasing
explanation: Reinterpreting pointers across unrelated types violates strict aliasing rules and is undefined behavior.

question: What is the value of `(unsigned short)(-1)` on a typical system?
options: 65535 on 16-bit systems only
65535 (2^16 - 1) on all systems
-1 stored as a signed value
implementation-defined
explanation: Converting -1 to unsigned fills all bits to 1, yielding the maximum unsigned value for that type.

question: Why does `void*` require explicit cast to other pointer types, but arrays and functions decay?
options: arrays and functions are not pointers
void* is generic but loses type info; decay preserves the type
C++ forbids implicit narrowing from void to specific types
this is a compiler quirk with no deep reason
explanation: Implicit void* conversion would hide type information; decay and decay-to-pointer are explicit type operations that preserve safety.

question: What happens if an exception is thrown but not caught?
options: the exception is silently ignored
the program calls std::terminate
the program continues normally
compilation error
explanation: An uncaught exception causes std::terminate to be called, which by default aborts the program.

question: Can you throw an exception from a destructor?
options: yes; destructors support exceptions
no; it is undefined behavior
yes, but it causes std::terminate during unwinding
only in C++11 onwards
explanation: Throwing from a destructor during stack unwinding causes std::terminate; it is technically allowed but dangerous.

question: What does the `noexcept` specifier guarantee?
options: the function never throws exceptions
the compiler prevents exception throwing in the function
if an exception is thrown, std::terminate is called
it is only a documentation hint
explanation: noexcept promises no exceptions; if one occurs, std::terminate is invoked without unwinding.

question: Can you catch a base class exception and rethrow it as a derived class exception?
options: yes; exceptions are polymorphic
no; the derived type is not available
only if explicitly cast
yes; but rethrow without new loses data
explanation: Catching by base type slices the exception; rethrowing a new derived exception loses original context.

question: What is the difference between `catch (std::exception e)` and `catch (const std::exception& e)`?
options: no difference; both catch the same exceptions
first copies the exception; second references it
second is safer and prevents slicing
both prevent slicing if derived exception is thrown
explanation: Catching by value slices derived exceptions; catching by const reference preserves the actual type.

question: Does a try block need a corresponding catch block?
options: yes; every try must have a catch
no; try without catch is valid if there is a function-try-block
only if the try block contains throwing code
error in C++
explanation: try without catch is valid in limited contexts; more commonly, at least one catch or resource handler is needed.

question: What does `catch (...)` do, and should it be used?
options: catches all exceptions; safe to use for cleanup
catches all exceptions; use sparingly for logging
syntax error
deprecated in C++11
explanation: catch (...) catches all exceptions, even non-std::exception types; useful for cleanup but can hide bugs if used carelessly.

question: If a constructor throws an exception, is the destructor called?
options: yes; destructors always run
no; the object is not fully constructed
only if the exception is caught
only for member objects, not the main object
explanation: If the constructor throws before the object is fully constructed, the destructor does not run; cleanup must use RAII.

question: What is the purpose of std::exception::what()?
options: returns a description of the exception
checks if an exception occurred
rethrows the exception
converts the exception to a string type
explanation: what() returns a const char* describing the exception; useful for logging and debugging.

question: Can you throw an exception in a const member function?
options: no; const functions cannot modify state
yes; throwing does not modify state
only if the exception is caught
error in C++
explanation: const prevents state modification but not exception throwing; exceptions are valid in const member functions.

question: If a function is declared but never defined, and it's never called, does the linker error?
options: yes; linker always requires definition
no; linker only checks called functions
yes; but only in release builds
yes; but only if ODR is enforced
explanation: The linker only reports missing symbols for functions that are actually called; unused declarations are ignored.

question: What is the output of a function that returns a reference to a local variable?
options: the value the local had before returning
undefined behavior on dereferencing the reference
compilation error
the reference is valid until the function ends
explanation: Returning a reference to a local creates a dangling reference; dereferencing it invokes undefined behavior.

question: Can two functions have the same name if they differ only in return type?
options: yes; function signature includes return type
no; return type is not part of the signature for overload resolution
yes in C++17 onwards
only for virtual functions
explanation: Function overload resolution ignores return type; return-type-only differences cause redefinition errors.

question: What does `int f(const int x)` mean for the caller, and how does it differ from `int f(int x)`?
options: caller must pass const int; otherwise compilation error
no difference in caller behavior; const is applied to the copy inside f
caller cannot modify x after function returns
const here is an error
explanation: const on value parameters is ignored by callers; both signatures are equivalent and the const is internal to the function.

question: If a function has a default argument, can the non-default version also exist?
options: yes; both overloads can coexist
no; it creates ambiguity
yes, but caller must call with all arguments explicit
only if declared in different scopes
explanation: Having both f(int x) and f(int x = 5) causes ambiguity when called with f(3), creating a compiler error.

question: What happens if you declare a function with ellipsis (`...`) but don't use va_list?
options: compilation error
valid; variadic function with type checking disabled
undefined behavior if called with extra arguments
the ellipsis is ignored
explanation: Ellipsis declares a variadic function without type-safe access; calling it with extra arguments is allowed but unsafe.

question: Can you take the address of an inline function?
options: no; inline functions have no address
yes; inline is a hint to the compiler, not a restriction on addresses
only if the function is not actually inlined
only in debug builds
explanation: inline is merely an optimization hint; the address of an inline function is still valid and usable.

question: If a function is declared static, where is it visible?
options: visible in the current translation unit only
visible globally with mangled name
visible to the entire program
error; static functions do not exist
explanation: static on a function at file scope limits visibility to that translation unit (internal linkage).

question: What is the difference between `void f()` and `void f(void)` in C++?
options: no difference; both take no parameters
f(void) is a C style; C++ ignores void
f() may take any parameters; f(void) takes none
f(void) is invalid in C++
explanation: In C++, both void f() and void f(void) declare a function with no parameters; f(void) is accepted for C compatibility.

question: Does a recursive function call count toward stack depth, or does the compiler optimize tail calls?
options: recursion always uses stack depth
compiler may optimize tail calls to loops, but no guarantee
C++ standard requires tail-call optimization
tail recursion is impossible in C++
explanation: Tail-call optimization is not guaranteed by the standard; stack depth depends on the compiler and optimization level.

question: What is the result of `delete nullptr`?
options: undefined behavior
compilation error
no-op; safe to delete nullptr
undefined until runtime
explanation: Deleting a null pointer is explicitly allowed by the standard and does nothing; it is safe.

question: What is a memory leak, and how does it occur?
options: allocated memory that is never freed
freeing memory multiple times
using memory after delete
all of the above
explanation: A leak is allocated memory that becomes unreachable and is never freed, wasting resources.

question: If new fails to allocate memory, what does it do?
options: returns nullptr
throws std::bad_alloc
returns an invalid pointer
undefined behavior
explanation: The default new throws std::bad_alloc on failure; nothrow new returns nullptr instead.

question: Can you use delete on memory allocated with malloc?
options: yes; both are interchangeable
no; must use free for malloc
yes; but only in debug builds
undefined behavior
explanation: malloc and delete are incompatible; malloc requires free, new requires delete.

question: What is the difference between `delete p` and `delete[] p`?
options: delete[] is faster
delete[] calls destructors for all array elements
both are identical; [] is ignored
delete[] is for arrays; delete for single objects
explanation: delete[] invokes destructor for each element; delete assumes single object, causing undefined behavior if used on arrays.

question: What happens if you access memory after calling delete on it?
options: safe; the memory is still accessible
undefined behavior; the memory may be reused
always causes a crash
platform-dependent
explanation: Use-after-free is undefined behavior; the freed memory may be reused or inaccessible, causing crashes or data corruption.

question: Does setting a pointer to nullptr after delete prevent use-after-free?
options: yes; nullptr check prevents access
no; other pointers to the same memory exist
partially; prevents accidental reuse by that pointer
completely; nullptr is always safe
explanation: Setting to nullptr prevents use via that specific pointer, but does not help if other pointers to the same memory exist.

question: What is the purpose of placement new?
options: allocates memory at a specific address without calling new
reserves memory in advance for performance
allocates on the heap with a specific alignment
allocates stack memory with delete compatibility
explanation: Placement new constructs an object at a pre-allocated address, separating allocation from construction.

question: Can global variables allocated with new be leaked if the program exits?
options: yes; memory is never freed
no; OS reclaims all memory on exit
depends on the operating system
depends on whether they are referenced
explanation: The OS reclaims all process memory on exit; leaked globals do not persist, but leaks in running programs still matter.

question: What is double-delete, and why is it dangerous?
options: calling delete twice on the same pointer
deleting two pointers in sequence
a compiler optimization technique
only dangerous in C++98
explanation: Double-delete calls destructors twice and may corrupt memory management structures, causing undefined behavior.

question: What is a race condition, and how can it occur?
options: multiple threads access the same variable without synchronization
threads execute in the wrong order
a thread crashes before finishing
threads are created too quickly
explanation: Race conditions happen when multiple threads read/write shared data without synchronization, producing unpredictable results.

question: What does std::mutex do, and when should it be used?
options: prevents threads from starting
serializes access to shared data via lock/unlock
makes data immutable to all threads
detects data races automatically
explanation: mutex ensures only one thread accesses protected data at a time, preventing race conditions.

question: What is deadlock, and how can std::lock help prevent it?
options: thread waits forever for a resource
two threads lock mutexes in opposite order; std::lock acquires all at once
thread is prevented from modifying data
deadlock is impossible in C++
explanation: Deadlock occurs when threads wait for each other's locks; std::lock atomically acquires multiple mutexes in a safe order.

question: What is RAII-based lock management, and why is it safer than manual unlock?
options: locks are created on the stack and destroyed automatically
manual unlock is always called
RAII prevents race conditions
RAII is only for destructors
explanation: std::lock_guard acquires the lock in constructor and releases in destructor, ensuring unlock even if an exception occurs.

question: What does std::atomic do compared to a mutex-protected variable?
options: atomic allows multiple threads to write simultaneously
atomic provides lock-free atomic operations on single variables
atomic is slower than mutex
atomic prevents all multithreading issues
explanation: atomic enables hardware-level indivisible operations without locks, suitable for simple flags and counters.

question: What is the difference between std::thread::join and std::thread::detach?
options: join waits for thread to finish; detach lets it run independently
both wait for completion; join is named differently
detach stops the thread immediately
only one can be called per thread
explanation: join blocks until the thread finishes; detach releases it to run independently, losing synchronization.

question: What happens if a std::thread object is destroyed without calling join or detach?
options: the thread continues running
std::terminate is called
the thread is automatically joined
behavior is undefined
explanation: Destructing a joinable thread calls std::terminate to prevent accidental resource leaks.

question: What does std::condition_variable do?
options: it is a lock for multiple threads
threads wait for a specific condition to be signaled
it validates data types at compile time
it prevents race conditions automatically
explanation: condition_variable allows threads to efficiently wait for events and be notified when conditions change.

question: What is a data race, and how does it differ from a race condition?
options: data race is when threads access data concurrently; race condition is outdated term
data race is undefined behavior; race condition is a logic bug
they are identical terms
data race only affects pointers
explanation: Data race is a memory safety violation (UB) when threads access data without synchronization; race condition is a logic bug.

question: Is it safe to call non-thread-safe functions from multiple threads without a mutex?
options: yes; the function handles concurrency internally
no; undefined behavior without synchronization
depends on whether the function is const
only unsafe for functions that modify data
explanation: Non-thread-safe functions must be synchronized externally; calling them concurrently without protection is undefined behavior.

question: What does slicing mean, and when does it occur?

undefined behavior when pointers cross class boundaries
a memory optimization technique in virtual inheritance
creating a shallow copy of an object
explanation: Object slicing occurs when a derived object is assigned to a base class variable by value, losing derived-specific data.

question: If a base class has a virtual function, must derived classes override it?
options: yes; all derived classes must implement it
no; derived class can inherit the base implementation
no; compiler forbids inherited virtual functions
only if explicitly marked with override
explanation: Virtual functions are inherited; a derived class is not required to override, and will use the base implementation if not.

question: What is the difference between private and protected inheritance?

protected derives inherit base public as protected; private inherits all as private
private inheritance is illegal in C++
they are identical but protected is preferred
explanation: private inheritance hides all base members from further derived classes; protected inheritance preserves protected access.

question: Can a destructor be virtual, and why?

only in abstract base classes
explanation: Virtual destructors ensure the derived destructor runs when deleting a derived object via a base pointer.

question: If a class defines a move constructor, does the compiler still generate a copy constructor?

only if copy constructor is explicitly deleted
depends on whether the class has a destructor
explanation: Defining a move constructor suppresses the compiler-generated copy constructor; you must explicitly default it if needed.

question: What is the purpose of pure virtual functions?
options: to force derived classes to implement them
to define an interface without implementation
to optimize performance by eliminating vtable overhead
to prevent instantiation of the class
explanation: Pure virtual functions (`= 0`) ensure derived classes override them; a class with any pure virtual cannot be instantiated.

question: Can you call a virtual function from a constructor, and will it dispatch to the derived version?
options: yes; virtual dispatch always occurs
no; compilation error in constructor
no; the base version runs because derived object is not fully constructed
yes, but only in C++17 onwards
explanation: During construction, the object is considered its current class type, not the final derived type; virtual calls dispatch to the base version.

question: What is the purpose of the override keyword, and is it required?
options: marks a function as overriding a base virtual; not required but recommended
overrides base implementation; required in C++11
allows overriding of non-virtual functions
error if base function is not actually virtual
explanation: override is optional but forces a compiler error if the base virtual is missing; aids clarity and catches mistakes.

question: In multiple inheritance, what problem can the diamond pattern create?
options: memory waste from duplicate base data
ambiguous virtual function calls
both; unless virtual inheritance is used
no problem; C++ handles it transparently
explanation: Diamond inheritance can duplicate base data and cause ambiguity; virtual inheritance ensures a single shared base.

question: What does `final` on a class declaration do?
options: prevents the class from being inherited
prevents virtual functions from being overridden
marks the class as unchangeable
syntax error in standard C++
explanation: final on a class forbids deriving from it; attempting to create a derived class causes a compiler error.

question: What is the output of `int x = 5; cout << (x++ + ++x);`?
options: undefined behavior
explanation: The order of evaluation of x++ and ++x is unspecified; modifying x multiple times without an intervening sequence point triggers undefined behavior.

question: Why does `operator==` often return `const bool` rather than just `bool` in a user-defined class?
options: to prevent assignment to the result
to allow chaining comparisons
historical legacy from older C++ versions
no valid reason; it is a mistake
explanation: Returning const prevents accidental assignment like `if ((a == b) = true)`, though modern code often omits it.

question: What is the difference between `a && b` and `a & b` when both are bools?
options: no difference; both are bitwise operations
&& short-circuits and returns bool; & always evaluates both and performs bitwise AND
& is faster due to no short-circuit overhead
they are identical and & was deprecated
explanation: Logical && short-circuits and returns bool; bitwise & evaluates both operands and returns the bit-wise AND result.

question: Given `struct S { int* p; }; S a, b; a = b;` what happens to memory?
options: deep copy of pointed-to data
shallow copy; both now point to same int
memory leak in a.p
compilation error without copy assignment
explanation: Default copy assignment performs shallow copy of struct members; both a.p and b.p now alias the same int.

question: What does `sizeof(a + b)` do when a and b are ints, and why is this useful?
options: computes sizeof the sum result
computes size of int without evaluating a + b
syntax error
returns the size of the temporary result at runtime
explanation: sizeof is a compile-time operator that does not evaluate its argument; it queries the type of a + b without running code.

question: In `a[i] = b[i++]`, which index is written: the old value of i or the new value?

new value; increment happens before assignment
undefined behavior due to sequence point violation
both sides use the old value, then i increments

question: What is the result of `5 / 2` vs `5.0 / 2` in C++?
options: both are 2.5
2 vs 2.5 due to integer division
2.5 vs 2 due to integer promotion
undefined until runtime
explanation: Integer division truncates: 5 / 2 = 2; floating-point division: 5.0 / 2 = 2.5.

question: Can you overload `operator&&` to short-circuit like the built-in version?

no; both operands are always evaluated in overloaded version
yes, but requires special compiler flag
no; operator&& cannot be overloaded at all
explanation: Overloaded operators lose short-circuit evaluation; both operands are passed as function arguments before the call.

question: What is the difference between prefix `++a` and postfix `a++` for efficiency?
options: no difference; compiler optimizes both equally
prefix creates no temporary; postfix creates a temporary copy
postfix is always faster
difference only exists for classes, not built-in types
explanation: Postfix returns the old value (requires a temporary), while prefix returns a reference to the modified object.

question: Given `const int a = 5; int& r = const_cast<int&>(a);`, is this safe to execute?

unsafe; modifying r invokes undefined behavior
unsafe but safe if a is in writable memory
compilation error
explanation: const_cast removes const, but if the original object is truly const, modifying it is undefined behavior.

question: What is the difference between pass-by-value and pass-by-reference in terms of performance?
options: both have identical performance
pass-by-value copies the object; pass-by-reference passes an address
pass-by-value is faster for large objects
pass-by-reference requires manual memory management
explanation: pass-by-value copies (expensive for large objects); pass-by-reference passes an address pointer (cheaper).

question: Why is cache locality important for performance?
options: it reduces memory allocation overhead
CPUs fetch memory in cache lines; sequential access is faster than random
it eliminates the need for synchronization
cache locality is irrelevant to modern CPUs
explanation: Cache lines fetch adjacent memory; sequential access within a cache line is orders of magnitude faster than cache misses.

question: When is inlining beneficial, and when might it harm performance?
options: inlining is always beneficial
beneficial for small functions; harmful if code bloat exceeds cache capacity
inlining only helps in debug builds
inlining has no effect on performance
explanation: Inlining small functions saves call overhead; inlining large functions causes code bloat and cache misses.

question: What is branch prediction, and why does it matter?
options: branches are predicted at compile time
CPUs predict which branch will execute; mispredictions cause pipeline flushes
branch prediction is only relevant for interpreters
all branches have identical performance
explanation: Modern CPUs speculate on branches; mispredictions cause expensive pipeline flushes, degrading performance.

question: Is it faster to use std::move on objects in performance-critical code?
options: always yes; move is free
yes for large objects; move avoids copying
no; move has same cost as copy
depends on compiler flags
explanation: Move transfers ownership without copying; crucial for large objects, but negligible for small POD types.

question: What is the purpose of link-time optimization (LTO)?
options: prevents linker errors
enables optimization across translation units at link time
makes executable files smaller
only available in C++20
explanation: LTO allows the compiler to inline and optimize across module boundaries, improving performance at the cost of link time.

question: Why might iterating over a std::vector be faster than iterating over a std::list?
options: vector iteration has fewer branches
vector uses contiguous memory; better cache locality than list's scattered nodes
list is intentionally slow
both have identical performance
explanation: Vector's contiguous layout fits cache lines; list's node pointers cause cache misses, even with similar algorithmic cost.

question: What is false sharing, and how can it degrade multithreaded performance?
options: threads share code sections
multiple threads' variables fit in one cache line, causing unnecessary invalidations
sharing data across threads is always false
false sharing is prevented by mutexes
explanation: If two threads modify unrelated variables on the same cache line, each modification invalidates the other's cache, causing stalls.

question: Is using smart pointers slower than raw pointers?
options: yes; smart pointers always add overhead
no; modern compilers optimize smart pointers to raw pointer performance
yes, but only for unique_ptr

explanation: Compiler optimizations eliminate smart pointer abstraction overhead; modern code sees no performance difference.

question: Why might const references be preferred to const pass-by-value for large objects?
options: const prevents optimization
const reference avoids copying; pass-by-value copies the entire object
they have identical performance
only matters for very large objects
explanation: const reference eliminates a copy; for large objects like vectors or strings, this difference is significant.

question: What does unique_ptr guarantee about ownership?

only one unique_ptr owns the object at any time
unique_ptr is shared across threads
ownership is transferred on copy
explanation: unique_ptr enforces exclusive ownership; moving transfers it, copying is forbidden to maintain uniqueness.

question: What is the difference between unique_ptr and raw pointers in terms of safety?
options: both require manual deletion
unique_ptr automatically deletes; raw pointers require manual management
both are equally safe
raw pointers are safer if used correctly
explanation: unique_ptr uses RAII to automatically delete on scope exit, eliminating manual cleanup and leaks.

question: Can a unique_ptr be copied, or only moved?
options: can be copied freely
can only be moved
copying creates a deep copy
depends on the custom deleter
explanation: unique_ptr cannot be copied (copy constructor and assignment are deleted) to maintain exclusive ownership.

question: What happens when two shared_ptrs reference the same object and both go out of scope?

object is deleted when the last shared_ptr is destroyed
object is never deleted
behavior depends on compiler
explanation: shared_ptr uses reference counting; the object is deleted only when the reference count reaches zero.

question: What is a circular reference, and how does it affect shared_ptr?

circular references are impossible with smart pointers
only affects unique_ptr
explanation: Circular references prevent reference counts from reaching zero; both objects leak unless broken with weak_ptr.

question: What does weak_ptr do, and when should it be used?

weak_ptr breaks circular references without keeping objects alive
weak_ptr is unsafe and should be avoided
weak_ptr only works in C++17
explanation: weak_ptr observes shared_ptr without incrementing reference count; used to break cycles and avoid leaks.

question: Can you convert a unique_ptr to a shared_ptr?

Use a firewall to block header inspection
Change the version number in package.json
explanation: Hiding version headers is a minor defense; real security comes from keeping Express and dependencies updated and fixing known vulnerabilities.

question: A route returns res.json(user) where user includes user.password (hashed). Should the password be included in the API response?
options: Yes; the password is hashed, so it's safe to expose
No; even hashed passwords shouldn't be in API responses, only verification is needed server-side
Yes, if sent over HTTPS
Only for admin users
explanation: Never return hashed passwords in API responses; they're not needed for authentication and increase attack surface if a client is compromised.

question: CORS is enabled: app.use(cors()). Any origin can now make requests. A malicious site initiates a request to your API. What's at risk?
options: CORS is only a convenience feature; there's no security risk
The malicious site can make authenticated requests if the user is logged in, leading to CSRF attacks
The malicious site can access your API key from headers
CORS vulnerabilities always result in data breaches
explanation: Unrestricted CORS allows any site to make requests with user credentials, enabling CSRF; restrict origins to trusted domains.

question: Rate limiting isn't implemented, and a hacker sends 1000 requests per second to /login, trying passwords. Why is this a problem?
options: The server is fast enough to handle it without slowdown
Brute-force attacks can crack weak passwords; rate limiting slows down attempts
Express logs all requests, so the attack is traceable
It only affects the API endpoint, not the database
explanation: Without rate limiting, brute-force attacks can guess passwords; implement rate-limit middleware to cap requests per IP/user per time interval.

question: An API accepts file uploads: app.use(express.json({limit: '50mb'})). A hacker uploads a 100MB file. Why could this be problematic?
options: The file is automatically rejected because it exceeds 50MB
Without a size check, large uploads can exhaust server memory or disk space (DoS)
Express prevents file uploads larger than the JSON limit
The file is silently truncated to 50MB
explanation: Large files without proper limits can cause denial-of-service; set appropriate upload limits and validate file types server-side.

question: res.set('X-Frame-Options', 'DENY') prevents clickjacking. A user visits a malicious site that embeds your API response in a hidden iframe. What's prevented?
options: The API data is encrypted before the iframe loads
The browser respects the header and prevents framing, blocking the attack
The clickjacking payload is blocked by the firewall
The malicious site can't access the X-Frame-Options header
explanation: X-Frame-Options header tells browsers to prevent framing by other origins, stopping attackers from using iframes to trick users into actions.

question: User input is logged: console.log('User:', req.query.user). A hacker sends ?user=. The log contains the XSS payload. Why is logging user input risky?
options: The log file becomes too large
If logs are viewed in a web dashboard without escaping, the XSS executes in the admin's browser
Console.log is deprecated and shouldn't be used
User input is always sanitized before logging
explanation: Unescaped user input in logs can execute XSS if logs are viewed in a web UI; sanitize or JSON-encode before logging.

question: A database query is executed in a route handler: const user = db.users.find({id: 1}). The handler sends res.json(user) immediately. Why might user be undefined?
options: The query completed successfully but found no matching record
The query is asynchronous, but the handler didn't await it
db.users.find() doesn't return a promise
The database connection is async and haven't been awaited
explanation: Async database queries return promises; if not awaited, the variable holds the promise object, not the result, often appearing as undefined when sent.

question: const pool = new db.Pool() is called once at app startup. This connection pool is reused by all route handlers. Why is this pattern preferred over creating a new connection per request?
options: New connections are faster than reusing from a pool
Reusing connections avoids the overhead of repeated connection setup/teardown
Connection pools require less memory than individual connections
Each request requires its own isolated connection for security
explanation: Connection pooling maintains pre-opened connections, eliminating expensive handshake overhead per request and improving throughput.

question: A database operation takes 5 seconds to complete. The route handler awaits the query but doesn't call res.send() inside. After the await, res.json(result) is called. What's the risk?
options: The response timeout is exceeded and the connection is closed
Express automatically closes the connection after 30 seconds if no response is sent
If the query completes but the handler crashes before res.json(), the client waits indefinitely
The response payload is corrupted due to long delays
explanation: If the handler awaits a long-running query and then crashes before sending a response, the client hangs; wrap in try-catch and always send a response.

question: A pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ' + userId) is executed. Why is this dangerous even if userId appears to be a number?
options: String concatenation is slower than parameterized queries
SQL injection is possible if userId is user input, even from numbers
Express doesn't support string concatenation in queries
The query is cached and changes to userId are ignored
explanation: String concatenation in SQL is vulnerable to injection attacks; use parameterized queries like pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?', [userId]) to prevent SQL injection.

question: A transaction is started with db.beginTransaction(). After inserting data, res.json() is called before commit(). Why could this cause issues?
options: Sending a response commits the transaction automatically
res.json() can't be called inside a transaction
The transaction is still open and uncommitted if an error occurs after res.json(), potentially leaving the database in an inconsistent state
Transactions prevent res.json() from working
explanation: If you respond before committing, errors after the response won't trigger rollback; the transaction may remain open or commit incompletely.

question: const result = await pool.query(SQL); is used in one route, and in another route, the same query is executed without await. The second route sends res.json(result). What happens?
options: result is undefined because the query hasn't completed
result is a Promise object, not the query result
Express waits for the query to complete before sending the response
The response includes the Promise stringified as a string
explanation: Without await, result holds the Promise object, not the data; sending this as JSON results in an empty object {} or error depending on the JSON serializer.

question: A connection pool has a maximum of 10 connections. 15 concurrent requests all try to query the database. What happens to the 11th-15th requests?
options: They are queued and wait for a connection to become available
They immediately fail with a connection error
Express creates additional connections beyond the pool limit
The requests are dropped without error
explanation: Connection pools queue waiting requests; once a connection is freed, the next queued request uses it, preventing connection exhaustion.

question: pool.on('error', (err) => { ... }) listens for connection errors. A connection drops silently in the middle of a query. Will the error handler catch it?
options: Yes; the pool emits 'error' events for all connection issues
Only if the error occurs during query execution, not mid-transaction
The query's error callback will fire instead; the pool error handler won't
It depends on whether the connection is reused or discarded
explanation: Pool-level error handlers catch general connection issues; query-specific errors fire in the query callback or rejected promise, not the pool error handler.

question: const db = require('db-module'); is called once in app.js. The same db object is used by multiple routes. If a middleware modifies db.config, will other routes see the change?
options: No; each route gets its own copy of the db object
Yes; the db object is shared, and modifications affect all routes using it
Only if the modification is made before app.listen()
Modifications to db.config require restarting the server
explanation: A single db object is cached and reused; mutations to its properties are visible to all routes because they share the same reference.

question: A route handler calls await db.query('DELETE FROM users WHERE age > ?', [age]). No error is thrown, but rows aren't deleted. What's likely?
options: The query syntax is incorrect
The transaction wasn't committed (if in a transaction) or the query didn't match any rows
DELETE operations require special permissions not set up
Express prevents DELETE queries by default
explanation: A successful query doesn't guarantee rows were deleted; check result.affectedRows or verify the WHERE clause matches intended rows.

question: A route throws new Error('Database error'). No error-handling middleware is defined. What happens?
options: The error is silently ignored and the route continues
Express catches the error and sends a generic 500 response
The error message is logged to console but the app keeps running
The entire Express app crashes
explanation: Express has built-in error handling that catches thrown errors in sync routes and sends a 500 response; without custom error middleware, it uses the default handler.

question: An async route handler has no try-catch: app.get('/api', async (req, res) => { throw new Error(); }). Will the built-in error handler catch it?
options: Yes; Express wraps async routes automatically
No; promise rejections bypass Express error handlers
Only if the error is thrown before the first await
Only if app.use((err, req, res, next) => {...}) is defined
explanation: Express doesn't automatically catch promise rejections in async handlers; errors must be caught with try-catch and passed to next(err) or the promise rejection will crash the process (pre-Express 5.x).

question: Error-handling middleware is defined: app.use((err, req, res, next) => { res.status(500).send(err.message); }). A synchronous error is thrown in a route. Which middleware handles it?
options: All middleware processes the request normally; the sync error propagates
The error-handling middleware catches it because it has 4 parameters
Express built-in handler processes it; custom error middleware is skipped
The sync error bypasses the error-handling middleware
explanation: Express recognizes error-handling middleware by the 4-parameter signature (err, req, res, next); synchronous route errors are caught and routed to this middleware.

question: Error middleware calls next(err) after logging the error. What happens?
options: The error is passed to the next error-handling middleware
The error propagates to the client
next(err) is invalid; error middleware should send a response
The error is stored for later processing
explanation: Calling next(err) in error middleware passes the error to the next error-handling middleware in the stack, allowing chaining of handlers.

question: An error is thrown after res.send() has been called. The error-handling middleware doesn't trigger. Why?
options: Errors after res.send() are ignored by Express
res.send() sets a flag that prevents error handling
Once the response is sent, the request is complete and error handlers don't run
The error must be thrown before any response method is called
explanation: After any response method (send, json, etc.) executes, the response is committed; subsequent errors can't be handled via middleware because headers are already sent.

question: try { await db.query(...); } catch (err) { next(err); } passes the error to next(). The error-handling middleware receives it. What should it do?
options: Log the error and call next() again to propagate it further
Log the error and send an appropriate HTTP response like res.status(500).json({error: err.message})
Rethrow the error to keep it propagating
Call next(err) again to ensure the error reaches the built-in handler
explanation: Error-handling middleware should log, process, and send a client response; calling next() or re-throwing leaves the client hanging.

question: res.status(500).send(error) is called in error middleware, where error is an Error object. The response includes [object Object]. Why?
options: Error objects can't be sent directly; they must be stringified
res.send() converts objects to [object Object]; use res.json() for objects
The error doesn't have a toString() method
Express doesn't support Error object serialization
explanation: res.send() with an object doesn't serialize it like JSON; use res.json(error) or res.json({error: error.message}) to properly format error responses.

question: A route handler wraps db.query() in try-catch but doesn't call next(err) when an error occurs: catch (err) { res.status(500).json({error: 'Server error'}); }. Is this acceptable?
options: No; all errors must be passed to next(err) for consistency
Yes; catching and responding directly is a valid error-handling pattern
No; the handler must call next() after sending a response
Yes, only if the route is the last route before error middleware
explanation: Both patterns are valid: catch-and-respond locally or pass to error middleware via next(err); choose one consistently across your app.

question: process.on('uncaughtException', (err) => { console.error(err); process.exit(1); }) is set up. An unhandled rejection occurs in Express. Will this handler catch it?
options: Yes; uncaughtException covers all errors including promise rejections
No; unhandled rejections require a separate 'unhandledRejection' handler
Only if the rejection happens outside async functions
It depends on whether the app is in development or production mode
explanation: Promise rejections are different from uncaught exceptions; listen to 'unhandledRejection' event instead, or use error-handling middleware to catch them.

question: Error middleware logs err.stack but err.stack is undefined. The error was created manually: throw {message: 'Custom'}. Why?
options: Custom objects don't have a stack property
The stack property is only generated for Error instances, not plain objects
The stack was stripped during error propagation
err.stack is only available in development mode
explanation: Always throw Error instances, not plain objects; Error objects capture the stack trace at creation time for debugging, plain objects don't.

question: Your Express app calls app.use(middleware) multiple times with different handlers. You run two requests simultaneously. In what order are middleware functions called?
options: Both requests execute the middleware in parallel without order guarantee
Each request flows through middleware in the order they were registered, independently
Only the first registered middleware runs; others are skipped
Middleware runs in reverse order of registration
explanation: Each request flows through the middleware stack sequentially in the order registered; simultaneous requests have independent middleware chains.

question: An app.get() and app.all() both match the same route '/data'. If both are registered, why does only one handler execute?
options: app.all() has priority and skips app.get() handlers
app.get() has priority and skips app.all() handlers
Whichever is registered first executes; the second is ignored
Both execute in registration order unless next() is not called
explanation: Both handlers execute in registration order, but if the first handler sends a response without calling next(), the second never runs because the response is complete.

question: You set app.set('view engine', 'ejs') but a template still renders with another engine. What's the most likely cause?
options: app.set() was never called correctly
The file extension doesn't match the engine (e.g., file.pug with ejs engine)
The view directory is set to the wrong path
EJS package is not installed in node_modules
explanation: Express matches the file extension to the registered engine; if the template has the wrong extension, Express uses a different engine even if app.set() declared EJS.

question: app.disable('x-powered-by') should remove the 'X-Powered-By: Express' header, but it still appears in responses. Which debugging step would reveal the issue?
options: Check if a middleware is explicitly setting the header after disable()
Verify the HTTP version supports headers
Ensure the client supports receiving headers
Check if Express was compiled with headers enabled
explanation: app.disable('x-powered-by') removes Express's automatic header, but a middleware added after could re-set it; trace the middleware stack to find the culprit.

question: You create a custom middleware function that returns a function returning a function: (options) => (req, res, next) => { ... }. Why use this pattern?
options: It's faster than a normal middleware function
It allows configuration parameters to be set at startup, not per-request
Express requires all middleware to be triple-nested
It prevents res.send() from being called more than once
explanation: Higher-order middleware (HOF pattern) lets you pass configuration options when registering, capturing them in a closure for every request.

question: app.use('/api', router) mounts a router at /api. Inside the router, a route is defined as router.get('/users'). What is the full path to match requests?
options: /users
/api/users
/api/api/users
/routers/api/users
explanation: Mounted routers prepend their mount path, so /api + /users = /api/users for the full matching route.

question: You call app.engine('custom', customRenderFunction) and set app.set('view engine', 'custom'). A template renders but the customRenderFunction receives unexpected arguments. Why?
options: app.engine() always passes the same 3 arguments regardless of configuration
res.render() calls the engine with (path, options, callback); ensure your function signature matches
Custom engines can't receive options from res.render()
The file path is always passed as the second argument, never the first
explanation: res.render() calls the engine function with (path, options, callback); mismatch between expected and actual arguments causes undefined behavior.

question: An app.listen(port, callback) callback never fires. What's NOT a possible cause?
options: The port is already in use by another process
The port number is negative or exceeds 65535
A middleware threw a synchronous error before the app started
The callback is wrapped in a Promise that never resolves
explanation: Synchronous middleware errors occur during route definition, not during app.listen(); listen() will still fire its callback unless the port itself is problematic.

question: app.locals.user = {name: 'John'} sets a template variable. In a route, res.render('page', {user: {name: 'Jane'}}) is called. Which user object reaches the template?
options: app.locals.user (John), because it's set at the app level
res.locals.user (Jane), because it's passed directly to render()
Both are merged; the template receives {name: 'John', name: 'Jane'}
Neither; the template receives an empty object
explanation: res.render() options override app.locals; Jane's user object is rendered, because passed-in variables have higher precedence.

question: You register app.use(express.json()) but req.body is undefined in a POST handler. The Content-Type header is set to 'application/json'. What's the issue?
options: express.json() only works with Content-Type 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'
The request payload didn't reach the middleware (e.g., client sent no body)
You called app.use(express.json()) after the route handler
express.json() requires app.use(express.urlencoded()) first
explanation: Middleware must be registered before route handlers; if express.json() is registered after the route, it never parses the body for that route.

question: A callback-based async operation chains three `.then()` handlers. The second handler throws an error. Which handlers execute?
options: All three handlers execute sequentially
First handler executes, second throws and is skipped, third never executes
First and second execute, third catches the error
Second handler catches the error and prevents first handler from running
explanation: Promise chains break on unhandled errors; handlers after the throw do not execute unless explicitly caught with `.catch()`.

question: An arrow function is declared inside a method: `const obj = { method: function() { const arrow = () => this; } };`. What does `this` refer to inside the arrow function?
options: The obj object
The global object (or undefined in strict mode)
The function's own scope
The object that called method()
explanation: Arrow functions inherit `this` from their lexical scope; here the enclosing function is not called in object context, so `this` is global or undefined.

question: const obj = { a: 1 }; const { a, b = 5 } = obj; console.log(b);  What prints?
options: undefined
null
ReferenceError
explanation: Destructuring with default values assigns the default when the property is undefined; `b` is not in obj, so `b = 5` applies.

question: const arr = [1, 2, 3]; arr.forEach((v, i) => arr.splice(i, 1));  What is the final state of arr?
options: [1, 2, 3] (unchanged)
explanation: Mutating an array during iteration skips elements; splice removes each element as the iterator sees it, leaving only index 0 untouched.

question: A function uses both rest parameters and destructuring: const f = ({ a, ...rest }, ...args) => rest;  const result = f({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }, 10, 20);  What is result?
options: undefined
explanation: Object rest `...rest` collects unmatched properties after destructuring `a`; the function argument `...args` is separate and not returned.

question: const p = new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve(10), 100)); await p; console.log(p);  What logs?
options: Promise { 10 }
Promise { <pending> }
Promise { <fulfilled>: 10 }
explanation: After `await` resolves, `p` is still the Promise object; only its [[PromiseState]] is `fulfilled` with value 10.

question: Two functions: `const f = (x = 0) => x + 1; const g = (f) => f() + 1;`  What does `g(f)` return?
options: NaN
explanation: f() uses default x=0, returns 1; g adds 1 to that result, returning 2... wait, g() itself returns 2, not 1. Actually f() = 1, g(f) = 1 + 1 = 2... no, g receives f, calls f() which is 1, adds 1 to get 2. Let me recalculate: f(undefined) with default x=0 returns 0+1=1; g(f) calls f() which is 1, then adds 1, returning 2. So answer is 2.

question: const obj = Object.freeze({ a: 1, b: { c: 2 } }); obj.b.c = 3;  What is obj.b.c?
options: undefined
Error thrown
explanation: Object.freeze only shallowly freezes the top level; nested objects are not frozen, so mutation of obj.b.c succeeds silently.

question: A module exports `module.exports = { f: () => this.x };`. Another module imports it, stores it in a variable, and calls it. What is `this` inside f?
options: The module's exports object
The global object
undefined (in strict mode)
The caller's context
explanation: A function called without an explicit receiver (`obj.f()`) has `this` bound to global (or undefined in strict mode), not the exports object.

question: const map = new Map([['a', 1], ['b', 2]]); for (const key in map) console.log(key);  What prints?
options: a, b
Nothing
Enumerates all Map internal properties
explanation: for...in iterates over enumerable properties of an object; Map has no enumerable own properties, so nothing logs.

question: Middleware A calls next(), then Middleware B calls next(), then a route handler sends a response. What happens if Middleware A calls next() again after the handler completes?
options: next() triggers Middleware B again, creating an infinite loop
next() has no effect; calling it after the response is sent does nothing
Express throws an error 'Response already sent'
The response is sent twice, doubling the data
explanation: Calling next() after the response is sent is a no-op; Express doesn't error, but no further middleware runs because the response is complete.

question: A middleware logs req.method, then calls next(). Inside the next() callback, it tries to modify req.method = 'DELETE'. The route handler sees req.method as POST. Why?
options: next() doesn't return control to the middleware after the handler runs
Modifying req after the handler processes it has no effect on that handler
req.method is read-only and cannot be modified
Express creates a copy of req before the handler, so changes are lost
explanation: next() is not a callback function; it immediately passes control forward and doesn't return, so code after next() in the middleware won't run until the response is sent (if at all).

question: Error-handling middleware is defined as (err, req, res, next) => { ... }. It's registered after route handlers. A synchronous error is thrown in a route. Why doesn't the error handler catch it?
options: Synchronous errors are never caught by error middleware
Error middleware must be registered before route handlers to work
The error middleware must explicitly listen to thrown errors with process.on()
Synchronous errors in routes are auto-caught by Express only if async/await is used
explanation: Error-handling middleware must be registered after all other middleware and routes; if registered before routes, it won't catch route errors. Also, sync errors must be explicitly passed to next(err).

question: Middleware calls res.json({data: 'test'}), then res.send('more'). What happens?
options: Both methods send their data; the client receives both responses
res.send() throws an error because the response is already sent
Only res.json() sends; res.send() is silently ignored
res.send() overwrites the previous response
explanation: After res.json() sends the response, res.send() silently fails because the response is already sent; Express prevents double-sending with internal flags.

question: A middleware modifies req.headers.authorization and calls next(). The route handler logs req.headers.authorization. Will it see the modified value?
options: No; req.headers is read-only after the request enters Express
Yes; modifying req.headers affects the original object
Only if next() is awaited like await next()
Only if the modification is done before app.use() is called
explanation: req.headers is a mutable object; modifications in middleware persist through the request chain because they're on the same req object.

question: Middleware A takes 30s to complete before calling next(). Middleware B and the route handler then run. Meanwhile, another request arrives and goes through Middleware A again. Why don't they block each other?
options: Express queues requests and processes them sequentially
Each request has its own context; Middleware A's 30s timer is per-request, not shared
Node.js runs multiple threads, one per request
Express automatically skips slow middleware for new requests
explanation: Node.js is single-threaded but asynchronous; each request maintains its own stack, so waiting in Middleware A for the first request doesn't block the second's execution.

question: Custom middleware stores user data in req.user = {id: 123}. Later middleware tries req.user.name = 'John' but gets 'Cannot set property name of undefined'. Why?
options: req.user is read-only and cannot have properties added
The first middleware didn't assign req.user before the second middleware ran
req.user is set to null instead of an object
Each middleware gets a separate copy of req, so changes don't propagate
explanation: If the first middleware didn't execute or didn't set req.user, the second middleware sees req.user as undefined; ensure middleware runs in the correct order.

question: A middleware uses app.use(bodyParser.json({limit: '10kb'})). A POST request with a 5MB body is sent. Why does it fail?
options: The body is larger than the 10kb limit, so the parser rejects it
bodyParser silently ignores large bodies and req.body is undefined
Express rejects the request before it reaches middleware
The body is truncated to 10kb automatically
explanation: bodyParser enforces size limits; exceeding the limit raises a 413 Payload Too Large error and req.body is not set.

question: Middleware is registered as app.use('/api', middlewareFunc). A request to /users is processed. Does middlewareFunc run?
options: Yes; app.use() middleware runs for all routes regardless of path
No; the path prefix /api prevents the middleware from running for /users
Only if /users starts with /api
Yes, but only if a route is defined for /users
explanation: Middleware registered with a path prefix only runs for routes matching that prefix; /users doesn't start with /api, so middlewareFunc is skipped.

question: An async middleware is registered: app.use(async (req, res, next) => { await somePromise(); next(); }). An error is thrown inside somePromise(). Why doesn't the error handler catch it?
options: Async errors in middleware are always ignored by Express
The error is thrown but next() was already called before the promise rejected
Errors in async middleware must be caught with try-catch and passed to next(err)
Express doesn't support async/await syntax in middleware
explanation: Express doesn't automatically catch promise rejections; wrap async code in try-catch and call next(err) to trigger error-handling middleware.
